sections.title: Grounded conductors — how they are identified
sections.plain_explanation: Article 200 is about the grounded conductor, which in a house is usually the neutral. Its job in this article is identification: how a worker can tell, by color, marking, or terminal, which conductor is grounded so nobody lands it in the wrong place. It does not size the neutral — that work lives in Articles 210, 215, 220, and 250.
sections.on_the_job: Treat white and gray as a warning label, not a suggestion. Before you splice, land, or re-mark a conductor, check what it is actually connected to at both ends.
sections.figure_idea: A panel detail showing a white insulated neutral landed on the isolated neutral bar, a green ground on the ground bar, and a black hot on a breaker, each labeled.

sections.title: The neutral serves its own circuit
sections.plain_explanation:
A grounded (neutral) conductor belongs to the circuit it was run with. It may not be borrowed to carry return current for a different circuit, and a neutral from one circuit or system may not be shared with another unless the arrangement is one the Code specifically builds — the multiwire branch circuit being the common one in a house. Where a neutral is shared, every rule for that shared arrangement (same raceway or cable, grouped disconnecting means, identification) has to be followed end to end. A neutral picked up from a nearby box because it was handy is a violation and a shock hazard: switching off one breaker leaves the shared neutral still carrying the other circuit's current.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 200.4: No new rule here. The one-neutral-per-circuit limit stands, and a new note points you to 215.4, the place where feeders can share a common neutral. New informational note: for feeders that share one neutral, look to 215.4 for the allowance.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Troubleshooting rule: if you open a box and find a neutral spliced to a circuit it did not arrive with, stop and trace both ends before you land anything. On a multiwire circuit, killing one breaker does not make the neutral safe — that is why the two hots disconnect together (see the 210.4 page).
sections.figure_idea: Two circuits at one panel: one with its own neutral run beside it (correct), one borrowing a neutral from the circuit next door (crossed out).

sections.title: How a grounded conductor is marked
sections.plain_explanation: This section gives the ways a grounded conductor may be identified, and the method changes with conductor size. Smaller insulated conductors use a continuous white or gray outer finish, or white or gray with colored stripes other than green. Larger conductors may use that same finish, or be identified at terminations and accessible points in the ways the section allows.
sections.on_the_job: On rough-in, pick the right roll — do not plan to tape your way out of the wrong insulation color on small branch wiring. On larger feeders, mark every accessible point, not just the end you happen to be landing today.
sections.figure_idea: Three feeder conductors at a panel: black, red, and one wrapped with white tape at the end, with a note that small branch conductors use factory white or gray insulation.

sections.title: What white or gray insulation may be used for
sections.plain_explanation: White or gray insulation is reserved for the grounded conductor, with narrow exceptions the section spells out. The familiar field examples are a re-identified conductor in a cable assembly used as a hot for a switch loop or a 240V circuit, and flexible cord uses — and re-identification has to be permanent and visible where required. A white conductor is never free to be a ground; equipment grounds are green, green with yellow stripes, or bare.
sections.on_the_job: If you re-identify a white wire as a hot, mark it at every box where it appears and tell the trim crew. If you open a box and find an unmarked white on a switch or breaker, stop and trace it instead of assuming.
sections.sharma_note: Never backstab and never guess a re-identified white — Sharma crews trace it. See S-10 for conductor and termination practice generally.

sections.title: Terminal identification and polarity
sections.plain_explanation: Terminals tell you where the grounded conductor lands. On receptacles, switches, lampholders and other devices, the terminal for the grounded conductor is identified — a silver-colored screw, or a terminal marked with the word WHITE — while the ungrounded (hot) terminal is brass or dark colored, and the equipment-grounding terminal is green (that rule is 250.126, not Article 200). Polarity is the matching rule in 200.11: the grounded conductor goes to the identified terminal, never reversed. On a standard receptacle that puts the neutral on the longer slot and the hot on the shorter one, so a plug's wide blade lands on the neutral side. the screw shell of a lampholder is the grounded-conductor terminal (200.10(C)).
sections.on_the_job: Reversed polarity is one of the most common findings in older Florida houses: the receptacle works, but the tester shows the fault. Land white on silver, black on brass, green on green, and check with a polarity tester at final — a lamp lighting up proves nothing about polarity.
sections.figure_idea: Duplex receptacle from the back: silver screw with the white conductor, brass screw with the black, green screw with the ground, and the face slots labeled to match.

sections.title: Branch circuits — the circuits that feed the load
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 210 governs the final run of wiring that delivers power to lights, receptacles, and appliances. It sets circuit ratings, the protection people need from shock and arc faults, which dedicated circuits a dwelling must have, where receptacles and lights must go, and how much load a circuit may carry. Most of Sharma's rough-in and trim work is judged against this article.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 210.1: Article 210 now has a voltage ceiling: 1,000 volts for AC branch circuits and 1,500 volts for DC. Anything higher moved to the new Article 235. The scope and the article title now top out at 1,000 volts for AC and 1,500 volts for DC.
• 210.17: Assisted living facilities now join hotels and motels: guest rooms or suites that have a permanent cooking setup get the same branch circuits as a dwelling unit. Assisted living facilities are now named with hotels and motels; a unit there with a permanent cooking setup gets dwelling-unit branch circuits.
• 210.18: 10 amps is now a legal rating for multioutlet branch circuits, joining the 15-, 20-, 30-, 40- and 50-amp ratings. Multioutlet circuits get a new rating option, 10 amps, on top of the 15-, 20-, 30-, 40- and 50-amp ratings.
• 210.62: The 12-feet-per-receptacle count for show windows is gone. Receptacles now go along the window top so no point there is more than 6 ft from one. Space show window receptacles so every point along the window's top edge is within 6 ft of one.
• 210.2: The information concerning reconditioned equipment has been relocated by CMP- 2 from 210.15 to 210.2 as it applies to branch circuits.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Read a house plan through Article 210 first: protection, dedicated circuits, receptacle layout, then lighting outlets. That order catches the expensive misses before wire is pulled.
sections.sharma_note: S-01: on commercial work Sharma runs 20A minimum branch circuits — stricter than this article requires for dwellings.

sections.title: Multiwire branch circuits
sections.plain_explanation:
A multiwire branch circuit shares one grounded conductor between two or three ungrounded conductors taken from different phases or legs. Because the shared neutral only carries the unbalanced current when the hots are on opposite legs, landing both hots on the same leg can overload a neutral that has no breaker of its own. The article also requires a way to disconnect all the hots together at the panel and grouping so the shared set can be identified.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 210.4: The same-origin rule for multiwire branch circuits now points to 300.3(B)(4), which covers column-width panelboards whose neutrals land in an attached pull box. Hots and neutral of any multiwire branch circuit still begin in one panelboard or other distribution equipment.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Before you share a neutral, confirm the breakers are on opposite legs and tied or on a common-trip / handle-tied arrangement as required. In a 120/240V house panel, that means adjacent positions are not automatically opposite legs in every panel layout — check, do not assume.
sections.figure_idea: A two-pole breaker feeding a red hot, a black hot, and one shared white neutral to two receptacle runs, with the opposite-leg point circled.

sections.title: Identifying branch circuits — colors and directories
sections.plain_explanation: Branch circuits have to be identifiable where they are worked on. Where a building is fed by more than one nominal voltage system — a light-commercial building with both 208Y/120 and 480Y/277 is the common case — the ungrounded conductors of each system are identified by phase and by system, and the identification method has to be posted at each panelboard (or the conductors durably identified by another approved method an inspector can read). The trade color conventions are black, red, blue for 120/208V systems and brown, orange, yellow for 277/480V systems. In a house the same discipline shows up as an accurate panel directory: every breaker labeled for the load it actually serves. The panel-directory rule is 408.4(A) (every circuit and modification legibly identified as to its clear, evident and specific purpose), not 210.5. 210.5(C)(1) applies only where branch circuits are supplied from more than one nominal voltage system, and the identification method must be readily available or permanently posted at each branch-circuit panelboard. The color schemes (black/red/blue, brown/orange/yellow) are trade convention; the NEC does not mandate particular colors for ungrounded conductors.
sections.on_the_job: Write the directory as you trim the panel, not from memory at final. On a two-system commercial job, land the colors to the posted code from the first pull — re-identifying a pulled circuit with tape at every box is slower and gets missed.
sections.figure_idea: Panelboard door with the posted color-code card: two voltage systems, their phase colors, and a directory filled in circuit by circuit.

sections.title: Ground-fault protection for people
sections.plain_explanation: This section requires ground-fault protection in the places where a person, water, concrete, or the outdoors make a fault to ground most dangerous. Protection can be provided at the receptacle, at the breaker, or by a device feeding through to downstream outlets, as long as the outlet that needs protection actually gets it. The 2020 dwelling rule reaches further than older editions — see the next pages.
sections.on_the_job: Walk the job location by location, not room name by room name. A receptacle in an unfinished part of a basement, within reach of a sink, or in a laundry area is judged by where it sits, not by what the plan calls the room.
sections.sharma_note: S-07: Sharma protects 120V circuits at the breaker with dual-function breakers and installs standard tamper-resistant receptacles at points marked GFI. No GFCI receptacles.
sections.figure_idea: A house diagram with the GFCI locations shaded: bathroom, garage, outdoors, basement, kitchen, sink areas, laundry, and tub/shower areas.
sections.florida_note: Florida enforces NEC 2020 through the FBC 8th Edition (2023), for permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026; the FBC 9th Edition (2026) adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026. A local AHJ amendment controls over any general summary here.

sections.title: Dwelling locations that need GFCI protection
sections.plain_explanation:
For dwellings, this list covers receptacles in bathrooms, garages and certain accessory buildings, outdoors, crawl spaces, basements, kitchen areas covered by the list, near sinks, in boathouses, near tubs and showers, in laundry areas, and in indoor damp or wet locations. In NEC 2020 the rule applies to receptacles rated 125V through 250V on single-phase circuits of 150V to ground or less — that is why a 240V dryer or garage receptacle is no longer outside the rule. Measurement points matter: distances are taken from the sink, tub, or shower feature the list names.

The 2020 list, item by item — receptacles in:
• (1) Bathrooms
• (2) Garages, and accessory buildings with a floor located at or below grade level
• (3) Outdoors
• (4) Crawl spaces, at or below grade level
• (5) Basements — finished and unfinished areas alike in the 2020 edition
• (6) Kitchens — where the receptacles are installed to serve countertop surfaces
• (7) Sinks — where receptacles are installed within 6 ft of the top inside edge of the bowl of the sink, other than the areas listed above
• (8) Boathouses
• (9) Areas within 6 ft of the outside edge of a bathtub or shower stall
• (10) Laundry areas
• (11) Indoor damp or wet locations In 2020 the sink distance is measured from the top inside edge of the bowl (2017 measured from the outside edge). Item (2) in 2020 reads: garages, and accessory buildings with a floor at or below grade not intended as habitable rooms and limited to storage areas, work areas and similar areas.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 210.8: GFCI now covers every dwelling kitchen receptacle, ranges, ovens, cooktops, dryers and microwaves however they connect, and more dwelling outdoor outlets, with listed HVAC exempt until September 1, 2026. All dwelling kitchen receptacles need GFCI now, not just countertop ones (210.8(A)(6)). New (A)(7) adds sink areas with permanent food or drink prep.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Use the existing lookup items for the full location list instead of working from memory on a walk-through. Pay special attention to the 6 ft sink and tub/shower measurements and to unfinished basement and garage areas that a finished-room mindset misses.
sections.sharma_note: S-07: protection is at the DFN breaker, so a standard TR receptacle in one of these locations is protected even though the device itself has no test buttons. Do not swap in a GFCI receptacle. Scope note: S-07 covers the 120-volt points on this list. A 240/250-volt point on the list (other than the dryer, which is S-08) takes a 2-pole GFCI breaker — a single-pole DFN cannot protect it.
sections.figure_idea: A bathroom and kitchen plan with 6 ft arcs drawn from a sink edge and from a tub edge, shading every receptacle inside the arcs.

sections.title: Laundry areas — including the dryer receptacle
sections.plain_explanation: Item (10) on the dwelling list is laundry areas. Read together with the 2020 voltage range in 210.8(A), it covers the 250V dryer receptacle as well as the 120V washer receptacle. That is the code reason a modern Sharma dryer circuit needs ground-fault protection even though older Florida houses were built without it.
sections.on_the_job: Do not treat the dryer as exempt because it is 240V, and do not protect only the washer outlet. Check the whole laundry area, including a laundry closet in a hallway or garage layout.
sections.sharma_note: S-08: dryer circuit is a Siemens Q230GF, 30A 2-pole GFCI breaker. That is the locked Sharma catalog number — do not substitute an older dryer breaker note.
sections.figure_idea: A laundry closet showing a washer receptacle and a 4-wire dryer receptacle, both with a line back to the panel and the 2-pole GFCI breaker highlighted.

sections.title: GFCI locations outside dwellings
sections.plain_explanation:
Non-dwelling occupancies have their own GFCI list, covering bathrooms, kitchens, rooftops, outdoors, areas near sinks, indoor damp or wet locations, locker rooms with showers, garages, accessory buildings and service bays (other than vehicle exhibition halls and showrooms), crawl spaces at or below grade level, unfinished areas of basements, laundry areas, and bathtub and shower stall areas where receptacles sit within 6 ft of the outside edge of the tub or stall. The voltage and size limits in this subsection are not identical to the dwelling list, so a commercial job cannot be roughed from house habits alone. Kitchens in commercial work are judged by the article's own definition and equipment, not by whether food is sold there.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 210.8(B)(4): Added buffet serving areas to the list of locations requiring ground-fault circuit-interrupter (GFCI) protection in Section 210.8(B)(4).
• 210.8(B)(7): Added "cord-and-plug-connected fixed and stationary appliances" to the existing language for sink locations.
• 210.8(B)(13): Section 210.8(B) added a new numbered list item (13) dealing with aquariums and bait wells in areas that are other than dwelling units. This change requires that receptacles installed within 1.8 m (6 ft.) of aquariums, bait wells, and similar open aquatic vessels or containers be provided with ground-fault circuit-interrupter (GFCI) protection.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: On a commercial walk, list the wet and outdoor locations from the plans and the equipment schedule, then match each one to this subsection. Flag rooftop and service-bay receptacles early — they are the ones most often added late.

sections.title: Specific appliances that need GFCI protection
sections.plain_explanation:
Beyond location lists, this subsection points to 422.5(A): specific appliances need ground-fault protection wherever they are installed, in any occupancy, when rated 150 volts or less to ground and 60 amps or less. The 2020 list is automotive vacuum machines, drinking water coolers and bottle fill stations, cord-and-plug-connected high-pressure spray washers, tire inflation machines, vending machines, sump pumps, and dishwashers. The test is the appliance and its rating, not the room. When an appliance is on the list, moving it to a room that is not on the 210.8(A) list does not remove the requirement.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 210.8(D): 210.8(D) now names the appliances: electric ranges, wall-mounted ovens, counter-mounted cooking units, clothes dryers and microwave ovens were added, correlated with 422.5(A).
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Check the appliance schedule, not just the room finish. If a listed appliance will be cord-and-plug or hardwired within the stated limits, plan the protection before the panel schedule is finalized.
sections.sharma_note: S-07: a DFN breaker supplies this protection on 120V circuits, with a standard TR receptacle at the appliance where there is a receptacle.

sections.title: Outdoor outlets other than receptacles
sections.plain_explanation:
This subsection reaches outdoor outlets that are not receptacles — a point where current is taken for equipment, such as the disconnect feeding a hardwired condenser. For dwellings, all outdoor outlets other than those already covered as outdoor receptacles need GFCI protection for personnel when supplied by a single-phase branch circuit rated 150 volts or less to ground and 50 amperes or less. The NEC's own exception covers lighting outlets other than those in 210.8(C). For a one- or two-family dwelling, Florida resolves the condenser question directly: FBC-Residential §E3408.1 amends 210.8(F) with Exception No. 2 — GFCI protection is not required for listed and labeled HVAC equipment.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 210.8(F): Dwelling outdoor-outlet GFCI was expanded (garages with floors at or below grade, accessory buildings, boathouses) and Exception No. 2 exempts listed HVAC equipment until Sept 1, 2026. NFPA TIA Log 1924 proposed moving that date to Sept 1, 2028 (comment period closed Sept 9, 2026); whether it was issued is not confirmed here — check the AHJ.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Check the circuit rating first: on a dwelling, a single-phase circuit at 150 volts or less to ground and 50 amperes or less puts a hardwired outdoor outlet in this rule. Listed HVAC on a house falls under the Florida exception; plan on GFCI protection for other outdoor equipment.
sections.sharma_note: Sharma practice (tip, not an S-rule): condensers are normally on a standard 2-pole breaker sized to the nameplate maximum overcurrent protection. Confirm the AHJ — do not present that practice as a code exemption.
sections.figure_idea: A condenser pad with a hardwired whip to a disconnect, labeled 'outlet, not a receptacle,' and a callout to confirm the local position.

Outside that case — commercial work, unlisted equipment, other outdoor outlets — the AHJ for the job still governs.

sections.title: Branch circuits a dwelling must have
sections.plain_explanation:
This section is the circuit-count backbone of a house: enough branch circuits for the load, plus the named dwelling circuits the next pages cover. General circuits are spread so the load is divided, and the required small-appliance, laundry, bathroom, and garage circuits have their own limits on what else they may feed. A panel schedule that only counts spare spaces has not answered this section — the named circuits have to exist and serve the right outlets.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 210.11: The required 20-amp garage receptacle circuit is no longer limited to the required receptacles, added receptacles can use their own 15-amp-or-larger circuits, and one-bay garages can share it with equipment. The required 20-amp circuit can now serve every garage receptacle, not just the required ones, but still no other kinds of outlets.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Build the panel schedule from this section outward: named circuits first, then general area circuits, then spares. If a named circuit is feeding lights or another room, that is a rough-in error, not a labeling fix.
sections.sharma_note: Sharma often uses modest 15A area circuits for lights, fans, and general receptacles and reserves 20A circuits for the required dedicated loads. That is company practice, not a code minimum — and S-01 reverses it on commercial work.
sections.figure_idea: A draft panel schedule with the four named dwelling circuits highlighted at the top and general circuits below.

The required 20-amp circuit can now serve every garage receptacle, not just the required ones, but still no other kinds of outlets.

sections.title: The named dwelling circuits: kitchen, laundry, bathroom, garage
sections.plain_explanation:
This subsection names four things. At least two 20A small-appliance circuits serve kitchen, pantry, breakfast, and dining receptacles, with tight limits on other outlets. At least one 20A laundry circuit serves the laundry receptacle and nothing else outside that area. At least one 20A bathroom circuit serves bathroom receptacles, or — for a single bathroom only — may carry that bathroom's other outlets. And the 2020 edition adds a dedicated 20A garage circuit for the required garage receptacles, with a limited allowance for readily accessible outdoor receptacles.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 210.11(C)(4): The text was revised at Section 210. l l(C)(4), clarifying that 15-ampere branch circuits are permitted to serve receptacle outlets installed in a dwelling unit garage that are in addition to the receptacle outlets required by 210.52(G)(l).
• 210.11(C)(4): A new exception (4) was added to Section 210.l l(C)(4), permitting the 20- ampere circuit supplying a single-vehicle bay garage to supply other equipment in accordance with requirements in 210.23(A)(l) and (A)(2).
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Label these four on the panel schedule by their code job, not by a room nickname, and check the 'no other outlets' limits before adding a convenience receptacle to any of them. The single-bathroom exception is the trap: it does not let one circuit carry two bathrooms' receptacles plus lights.
sections.sharma_note: S-06 sits on top of this list: the microwave gets its own 20A circuit, separate from the small-appliance circuits. The wire size is PENDING (12 AWG copper versus 10 AWG CCA).

sections.title: Arc-fault protection
sections.plain_explanation: Arc-fault protection guards against damaged, pinched, or deteriorating wiring and loose connections that can arc long before a breaker sees an overload. The protection may be provided by a listed combination-type breaker or by one of the other arrangements the article permits, but the outlets in the listed rooms have to end up protected. Arc-fault and ground-fault protection do different jobs; one does not replace the other.
sections.on_the_job: Think of this as a room list applied at the panel. When a plan adds a room or changes a room's use, re-check the list instead of copying the last house's schedule.
sections.sharma_note: S-07: Sharma's dual-function breaker provides both arc-fault and ground-fault protection on every 120V circuit, so the room-by-room question is answered at the breaker for standard house work.
sections.figure_idea: A cutaway wall showing a nail through a cable with a small arc, and the breaker in the panel sensing the arcing signature.

sections.title: Rooms where dwelling circuits need AFCI protection
sections.plain_explanation: For dwellings, this subsection applies to 120V, single-phase, 15A and 20A branch circuits supplying outlets or devices in the listed rooms and areas — kitchens, family rooms, dining rooms, living rooms, parlors, libraries, dens, bedrooms, sunrooms, recreation rooms, closets, hallways, laundry areas, and similar rooms or areas. A bathroom, garage, or unfinished basement is not on this list. The rating limits matter too: a 240V appliance circuit is outside this subsection's stated range.
sections.on_the_job: On the panel schedule, mark every 15A and 20A 120V circuit with the rooms it serves, then test that list against this subsection. Mixed circuits that touch a listed room need the protection for the circuit.
sections.sharma_note: S-07 already puts a dual-function breaker on every 120V circuit, which is stricter and simpler than sorting rooms at trim. Keep it that way unless Sanjay directs otherwise on a specific job.

sections.title: Extending or modifying an existing circuit
sections.plain_explanation:
Where branch-circuit wiring in any area covered by 210.12(A), (B), or (C) — dwelling units, dormitory units, and guest rooms and guest suites — is modified, replaced, or extended, the circuit must gain AFCI protection. It may be protected by any of the methods in 210.12(A)(1) through (6), or by a listed outlet branch-circuit AFCI at the first receptacle outlet of the existing circuit. One narrow exception: no AFCI is required where the extension of the existing conductors is not more than 6 ft and adds no outlets or devices other than splicing devices; conductor length inside an enclosure, cabinet, or junction box does not count toward the 6 ft.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 210.12: AFCI now reaches sleeping quarters at stations for fire, police, ambulance, rescue and ranger crews, and 10-amp circuits join the 15-amp and 20-amp circuits that need it. Rooms used only for sleeping at stations for fire, police, ambulance, rescue or ranger crews, and similar places, now need AFCI (210.12(D)).
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: On service work, measure the extension before assuming the exception saves you: 6 ft or less, splices only, and no new outlet or device. Anything longer, or anything added, means AFCI — one of the 210.12(A) methods, or an outlet branch-circuit AFCI at the first receptacle.

nec2023_change.change: AFCI now reaches sleeping quarters at stations for fire, police, ambulance, rescue and ranger crews, and 10-amp circuits join the 15-amp and 20-amp circuits that need it. Rooms used only for sleeping at stations for fire, police, ambulance, rescue or ranger crews, and similar places, now need AFCI (210.12(D)).
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 210.12 AFCI protection

sections.title: Sizing branch-circuit conductors
sections.plain_explanation:
Conductors and breakers for a branch circuit are sized for the load the circuit will actually carry, and a continuous load — one that runs at its maximum for three hours or more — is counted at 125 percent for that sizing unless the assembly is listed for continuous operation at its rating. That is why a load that looks like it 'fits' a breaker on nameplate amps alone can still need the next size up. Multi-outlet circuits supplying receptacles for cord-and-plug loads are also sized by the rating rules in this section and in 210.23.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 210.19: Clarified that the voltage limitation should apply to the circuit, not the conductor insulation rating, and specified that Section 210.19 applies to branch circuits not exceeding 1000 volts ac or 1500 volts dc.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job:
Find the continuous loads first: EV charging, fixed heating, some lighting and equipment. Do the 125 percent math on paper in the job file, not in your head at the supply counter.

Worked example: a 16A continuous load counts 16 × 1.25 = 20A, so both the conductor ampacity and the breaker land at 20A minimum. A 24A continuous load counts 30A the same way — which is why an EV charger nameplate that 'fits' a smaller breaker on its face still sizes the circuit up.
sections.sharma_note: S-01: commercial branch circuits are 20A minimum with 12 AWG copper minimum at Sharma, whatever the general sizing math would allow at 15A.
sections.figure_idea: A worked example strip: 16A continuous load, times 1.25, equals a 20A circuit — with the breaker and the conductor both stepped up.

nec2023_change.change: Clarified that the voltage limitation should apply to the circuit, not the conductor insulation rating, and specified that Section 210.19 applies to branch circuits not exceeding 1000 volts ac or 1500 volts dc.
nec2023_change.source: Carosella/NFPA-based 2023 NEC change workbook: 210.19 Conductors - Minimum Ampacity and Size

sections.title: Outlet devices and receptacle ratings on a circuit
sections.plain_explanation:
This section matches the device to the circuit: lampholders, receptacles, and cord-and-plug equipment may not be loaded beyond their own ratings, and a receptacle's rating must fit the circuit it sits on. On a 20A multi-outlet circuit, 15A duplex receptacles are permitted because the load is spread across outlets; a single receptacle on an individual 20A circuit is a different case and must match the circuit. The existing lookup item carries the rating table in plain form.

The rating match, from Table 210.21(B)(3) — where a circuit feeds two or more receptacles, the receptacle rating may be:
• 15A circuit — receptacles not over 15A
• 20A circuit — 15A or 20A receptacles
• 30A circuit — 30A receptacles
• 40A circuit — 40A or 50A receptacles
• 50A circuit — 50A receptacles
A single receptacle on an individual branch circuit must be rated not less than the circuit. And the most one cord-and-plug load may draw on a multi-outlet circuit (Table 210.21(B)(2)):
• 15A circuit — 12A
• 20A circuit — 16A
• 30A circuit — 24A
sections.on_the_job: When a plan calls for a single dedicated receptacle — a fridge, a microwave, a shop tool — check the device rating against the circuit rating before trim. Do not let a trim bin of 15A devices decide the question.
sections.sharma_note: S-06: the microwave's individual 20A circuit pairs with that sizing check.

sections.title: How much load a branch circuit may carry
sections.plain_explanation:
This section caps what may be put on a circuit by its rating. Any one cord-and-plug-connected utilization equipment not fastened in place may not take more than 80 percent of the branch-circuit rating (12A on 15A, 16A on 20A) on any 15A or 20A branch circuit, and fastened-in-place equipment has its own limit when it shares a circuit with lighting or portable loads. Motor and specific-appliance loads are sent to their own articles instead of being judged by a general percentage.

The percentages in amperes:
• A cord-and-plug appliance that is not fastened in place, on a circuit that also serves other outlets — not over 80 percent of the circuit rating: 12A on a 15A circuit, 16A on a 20A circuit
• Fastened-in-place equipment sharing a circuit with lighting outlets or portable cord-and-plug loads — not over 50 percent of the circuit rating: 10A on a 20A circuit
A circuit that serves only its own fastened equipment is judged by the equipment's own article and nameplate, not by these shared-circuit caps. 7.5A on a 15A circuit, 10A on a 20A circuit

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 210.23: Only three things fit a 10-amp circuit: lighting, a dwelling bath or laundry fan on that room's lights, and a lone gas fireplace. Receptacles, laundry equipment, garage door openers and other fixed appliances stay off. Lighting outlets are the main job for a 10-amp branch circuit.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Do the percentage math for the big plug-in loads: space heaters, window units, and shop equipment are where a shared 20A circuit quietly goes over. If a load is fastened in place and shares the circuit, check the second limit too.

nec2023_change.change: Only three things fit a 10-amp circuit: lighting, a dwelling bath or laundry fan on that room's lights, and a lone gas fireplace. Receptacles, laundry equipment, garage door openers and other fixed appliances stay off. Lighting outlets are the main job for a 10-amp branch circuit.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 210.23 What a 10-amp circuit can feed

sections.title: Where dwelling receptacles must go
sections.plain_explanation:
This is the placement section: it decides where receptacles are required in a dwelling, room by room and surface by surface, so that cords stay short and extension cords stay out of daily use. It does not set circuit ratings — 210.11 does that — and it does not set a general mounting height for ordinary wall receptacles. The subsections that follow walk the house in the order Sharma roughs it: walls, counters, bathrooms, outdoors, laundry, garage, halls, and foyers.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 210.52: Dwelling kitchen islands and peninsulas don't need a receptacle anymore, and no countertop receptacle can sit below the top. Skip the island receptacle and you still leave provisions for one later. A receptacle at a kitchen island or peninsula is now optional.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Rough from this section with a tape and the floor plan, not from habit. Most placement callbacks are a missed wall, a missed bay, or a counter run measured from the wrong edge.
sections.sharma_note: S-04: where the plan is silent, receptacles are set 18 in to the bottom of the box. That is a Sharma standard, not a number from this section — countertop limits in 210.52(C) are code and are different.
sections.figure_idea: A floor plan with a receptacle symbol being placed along every wall, counter, and hallway in sequence.

nec2023_change.change: Dwelling kitchen islands and peninsulas don't need a receptacle anymore, and no countertop receptacle can sit below the top. Skip the island receptacle and you still leave provisions for one later. A receptacle at a kitchen island or peninsula is now optional.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 210.52 Island receptacles now optional

sections.title: Wall spacing in habitable rooms
sections.plain_explanation: In kitchens, family rooms, bedrooms, and the other rooms this subsection lists, receptacles are placed so that no point along the floor line of a wall is more than 6 ft from a receptacle — which works out to 12 ft maximum between receptacles on a run. Wall space is counted from 2 ft wide upward, and the section explains how fixed panels, sliding panels, and room dividers count, and when a floor receptacle may count toward the requirement. A receptacle behind a fixed appliance or too far above the floor does not do the job this spacing is meant to do.
sections.on_the_job: Measure along the floor line around corners and breaks, the way a lamp cord actually travels. Mark the 2 ft wall pieces — beside a door, between a closet and a corner — because those are the ones that get skipped.
sections.sharma_note: S-04 sets the box height when the plan is silent: 18 in to the bottom of the box. S-05 sets switch boxes at 48 in to center under the same condition.
sections.figure_idea: A wall elevation with a tape running along the floor line, arrows showing 6 ft maximum from any point to the nearest receptacle and 12 ft maximum between two.

sections.title: Small-appliance circuits — what they may feed
sections.plain_explanation: The two (or more) 20A small-appliance branch circuits serve the receptacle outlets in the kitchen, pantry, breakfast room and dining room — and only those. A receptacle for refrigeration equipment in those rooms may ride on one of them. The only other outlets allowed are a clock receptacle and receptacles used for supplemental equipment on a gas-fired range, oven or cooktop. A receptacle in the living room, a bathroom receptacle, or the kitchen lighting may not be added to these circuits, and these circuits may not wander off to feed outlets in other rooms. Refrigeration equipment may instead be fed from an individual branch circuit rated 15A or more (210.52(B)(1) Exception No. 2).
sections.on_the_job: Lay out the two circuits before rough-in so the countertop receptacles alternate between them (that layout rule is on the 210.52(C) page). Sharma rule S-06 puts the microwave on its own 20A circuit. Code-wise, a countertop microwave may plug into a small-appliance circuit; a fastened-in-place over-the-range microwave may not be fed from one (210.52(B)(2)).
sections.figure_idea: Kitchen plan with receptacles colored by circuit: countertop outlets split between SA-1 and SA-2, the fridge on SA-1, the microwave on its own circuit.

sections.title: Kitchen countertops, islands, and peninsulas
sections.plain_explanation:
Countertop receptacles are placed so no point along the wall line of a counter is more than 24 in from a receptacle, and a counter run 12 in or wider needs one. Islands and peninsulas are handled by counter area in the 2020 edition: one receptacle for the first portion of countertop area and one more for each additional stated increment — the existing checklist item carries the 2020 numbers. This subsection also limits how far above a counter a receptacle may sit and restricts receptacles placed face-up in a work surface to listed assemblies. A peninsular countertop also needs at least one receptacle within 2 ft of its outer end, measured from the connecting wall (210.52(C)(2)).

The island and peninsula count in numbers (2020 edition):
• One receptacle for the first 9 sq ft of island or peninsular countertop, or fraction of it
• One more receptacle for each additional 18 sq ft, or fraction of it
So a 30 sq ft island needs three: one for the first 9, and one each for the next 18 and the remaining 3. Two more placement numbers from this subsection:
• A receptacle installed above a countertop may sit no more than 20 in above the counter surface
• Countertop space separated by a range, cooktop, refrigerator, or sink counts as a separate countertop space — each separated run gets its own 24 in spacing check

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 210.52(C): Island and peninsula receptacles are no longer required. If installed they must be above or in the countertop/work surface (not on the side below the counter); if none is installed, a provision for a future receptacle must be provided at the island or peninsula.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Count island area from the actual countertop drawing, including an overhang that is part of the work surface, and confirm the count before rough-in — adding an island receptacle after cabinets are set is the expensive version. Under the 2020 rules an island or peninsula receptacle may sit on or above the counter, or below it — not more than 12 in below the countertop, where the counter extends not more than 6 in beyond its supporting base (210.52(C)(3)).
sections.figure_idea: An island drawn in plan with its countertop area shaded and divided into the first area block and the additional blocks, one receptacle marked per block.

nec2023_change.change: Island and peninsula receptacles are no longer required. If installed they must be above or in the countertop/work surface (not on the side below the counter); if none is installed, a provision for a future receptacle must be provided at the island or peninsula.
nec2023_change.source: NYEIA 2020/2023 residential changes (item 15); Electrical Exam Coach 210.52

sections.title: Bathroom receptacles
sections.plain_explanation: Each bathroom needs a receptacle close to every basin: within 3 ft of the outside edge of the basin, on a wall or partition next to it, or in one of the other positions this subsection permits. A double vanity has two basins and needs the requirement met for each one. This placement rule works alongside the bathroom circuit rule in 210.11(C)(3) and the GFCI list in 210.8(A) — all three have to be satisfied at the same sink.
sections.on_the_job: Measure from the basin's outside edge, not from the center of the faucet and not from the cabinet edge. On a long double vanity, one receptacle in the middle may not be within 3 ft of both basins — check both.

sections.title: Outdoor receptacles for a dwelling
sections.plain_explanation: A one- and two-family dwelling needs readily accessible outdoor receptacles at the front and at the back, no more than 6.5 ft above grade, and additional rules cover balconies, decks, and porches that are accessible from inside. Multifamily buildings have their own version of this requirement. 'Readily accessible from grade' is part of the rule — a receptacle that can only be reached by a ladder or through a locked gate area does not serve the purpose. The requirement applies to a balcony, deck, or porch of 20 sq ft or more in overall area that is accessible from inside the dwelling.
sections.on_the_job: Place the front and back receptacles where a person standing on the ground can actually use them, and check porches and decks on the plan for the extra receptacle. Height is measured from grade at that wall, which matters on a sloped lot.
sections.florida_note: Florida lots often slope toward drainage swales; measure the 6.5 ft from the grade at the receptacle, and confirm any local amendment with the AHJ.

sections.title: Laundry receptacles
sections.plain_explanation: At least one receptacle is required in the laundry area of a dwelling, and it is served by the laundry branch circuit covered in 210.11(C)(2). A laundry closet counts the same as a laundry room for this placement rule. The dryer receptacle is a separate, larger outlet — this subsection is about the general laundry receptacle, usually the washer.
sections.on_the_job: If the washer location moves on a plan revision, move this receptacle with it and keep it on the laundry circuit. A receptacle borrowed from an adjacent hallway circuit fails both placement and circuit rules.

sections.title: Garage receptacles — one per vehicle bay
sections.plain_explanation:
In the 2020 edition, a dwelling garage with power needs at least one receptacle in each vehicle bay, placed no more than 5.5 ft above the floor. Attached and detached garages are both addressed, and garages without electric power are outside the requirement. The bay rule replaced the older single-garage-receptacle habit — a three-bay garage is not finished with one receptacle by the door.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 210.52(G): Clarified that the receptacle provided for premises security systems did not meet the receptacle requirements of210.52(G).
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Count bays from the door layout on the plan, not from how the owner says they will park. Put one receptacle in each bay at rough-in; adding the third bay's receptacle at trim is a drywall patch.
sections.figure_idea: A three-bay garage in plan view with one receptacle symbol inside each bay outline and a 5.5 ft height note.

nec2023_change.change: Clarified that the receptacle provided for premises security systems did not meet the receptacle requirements of210.52(G).
nec2023_change.source: Carosella/NFPA-based 2023 NEC change workbook: 210.52(G) Basements, Garages, and Accessory Buildings

sections.title: Hallway receptacles
sections.plain_explanation: A dwelling hallway that is 10 ft or longer needs at least one receptacle. Length is measured along the centerline of the hallway, following its turns, without going through a doorway into another room. Short halls need none under this subsection, which is why the measurement — not a guess at 'about ten feet' — decides it.
sections.on_the_job: Run the tape down the centerline and around the bend of an L-shaped hall before deciding. Vacuum and night-light use is exactly what this receptacle is for.

sections.title: Foyer receptacles
sections.plain_explanation: A foyer that is not part of a hallway and is greater than 60 sq ft has its own receptacle rule: a receptacle outlet is required in each wall space 3 ft or more in width, on walls not interrupted by door openings, other openings, or similar architectural features. A smaller foyer, or a foyer that forms part of a hallway, is judged under the hallway rule in 210.52(H) or the spacing rule for the room it opens into instead.
sections.on_the_job: Measure the foyer as its own space when it is separated by doors or cased openings. Do not count a wall segment that is mostly doorway as usable wall space.

sections.title: A service receptacle near heating and air-conditioning equipment
sections.plain_explanation: Equipment that needs servicing needs a receptacle close to it: a 125V, 15A or 20A receptacle on the same level and within 25 ft of heating, air-conditioning, and refrigeration equipment. It may not be wired to the load side of the equipment disconnect, so it stays live for a work light and tools while the unit is shut off. Rooftop and attic equipment are the cases Sharma meets most.
sections.on_the_job: At rough-in, locate the air handler and condenser, then place the receptacle and prove the 25 ft with a tape — following the access path, not through a wall. Keep it off the equipment circuit's load side.
sections.figure_idea: An attic air handler with a receptacle on a joist nearby, a 25 ft arc drawn around the unit, and the disconnect shown with the receptacle wired ahead of it.

sections.title: Lighting outlets and wall switches
sections.plain_explanation:
Habitable rooms, kitchens, and bathrooms need a wall-switched lighting outlet; in some living areas a switched receptacle may stand in for it, and the subsection separates those cases. Hallways, stairways, attached garages, and entries have their own switch-location rules, and rooms and spaces used for storage or equipment, plus attics and similar spaces, have lighting requirements of their own. The point throughout is that a person should never have to cross a dark room or a dark stair to reach a switch.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 210.70: Dwelling laundry areas now need a wall-controlled lighting outlet, battery-only controls must fail with the lights on, outdoor doors need a real exterior light, and bulkhead doors got their own allowance. Dwelling laundry areas join habitable rooms, kitchens and bathrooms: each needs a lighting outlet on a listed wall-mounted control near an entrance (210.70(A)(1)).
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Walk the plan as a person arriving at night: front door, hall, stairs, each room. If any leg of that walk is in the dark, a switching rule has probably been missed.
sections.sharma_note: S-05: switch boxes at 48 in to center when the plan is silent.
sections.figure_idea: A stair section with a switch at the bottom landing, a switch at the top landing, and the light over the stair lit from either one.

nec2023_change.change: Dwelling laundry areas now need a wall-controlled lighting outlet, battery-only controls must fail with the lights on, outdoor doors need a real exterior light, and bulkhead doors got their own allowance. Dwelling laundry areas join habitable rooms, kitchens and bathrooms: each needs a lighting outlet on a listed wall-mounted control near an entrance (210.70(A)(1)).
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 210.70 Laundry lighting and battery controls

sections.title: Feeders — power between the service and the final panels
sections.plain_explanation:
A feeder carries power from service equipment, a transformer, or another source to the panelboards where branch circuits begin. Article 215 is short: it covers feeder conductor sizing, overcurrent protection, and ground-fault protection for certain large feeders. Most feeder questions on a Sharma job are really answered together with Article 220 for the load, Article 240 for the protection, and Article 250 for the grounding conductor that runs with it.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 215.15: Panelboards, switchboards, switchgear and motor control centers supplied through feeder taps or transformer secondaries now need barriers over line-side bus and terminals that stay live with the disconnect open.
• 215.18: New in 2023: a feeder that supplies a dwelling unit, dorm unit, hotel or motel guest room, or nursing home sleeping room needs a surge-protective device (SPD) at the panel it feeds. Feeders to dwelling units, dorm units, hotel or motel guest rooms and suites, and nursing home or limited-care patient sleeping rooms now need an SPD.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Name the run correctly on the schedule — service conductors, feeder, or branch circuit — because the sizing and grounding rules change with the name. A subpanel feed is a feeder, and it is wired like one.
sections.sharma_note: S-02 and S-09 frame Sharma feeder work: new gear is Siemens, and the house panel normally sits back to back with the meter where the house allows.
sections.figure_idea: A one-line diagram: meter and service disconnect, a feeder run, a subpanel, and branch circuits leaving the subpanel.

nec2023_change.change: Panelboards, switchboards, switchgear and motor control centers supplied through feeder taps or transformer secondaries now need barriers over line-side bus and terminals that stay live with the disconnect open.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 215.15 Barriers in tap-fed equipment

nec2023_change.change: New in 2023: a feeder that supplies a dwelling unit, dorm unit, hotel or motel guest room, or nursing home sleeping room needs a surge-protective device (SPD) at the panel it feeds. Feeders to dwelling units, dorm units, hotel or motel guest rooms and suites, and nursing home or limited-care patient sleeping rooms now need an SPD.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 215.18 Surge protection on feeders

sections.title: Feeder conductor size and the continuous-load rule
sections.plain_explanation: Feeder conductors must have ampacity at least as large as the noncontinuous load plus 125 percent of the continuous load, before derating and correction are worked through, unless a listed assembly rated for continuous operation is used. Feeders supplying a dwelling's whole load may also be sized under the dwelling service and feeder table covered in Chapter 3, which is why a house feeder is not always sized from the general ampacity table alone. The calculated load itself comes from Article 220.
sections.on_the_job:
Do the Article 220 number first, then size the feeder — never size from the size of the panel that happens to be on the truck. Write the continuous portion down separately so the 125 percent step can be checked.

Worked example: a feeder carrying 80A of noncontinuous load plus 40A of continuous load needs conductor ampacity of at least 80 + (40 × 1.25) = 130A before correction and adjustment factors are applied. If the math is not written down in that form, the 125 percent step is the part that gets lost.

sections.title: Feeder overcurrent protection
sections.plain_explanation:
A feeder is protected by an overcurrent device rated not over the ampacity of its conductors, subject to the allowances in Article 240 — including the next-higher-standard-rating allowance where it applies and the tap rules where it does not. The breaker at the start of the feeder is therefore a conductor-protection question first and a load question second. Where a feeder continues to a subpanel, the equipment grounding conductor and the neutral treatment at that subpanel are Article 250 questions, covered later in this chapter.

The feeder's equipment grounding conductor is part of the feeder: it is sized from Table 250.122 by the rating of this overcurrent device and run with the feeder conductors. Where the feeder supplies a separate building, the grounding arrangement at that building follows 250.32 — this device's rating still sets the equipment grounding conductor size. Where a feeder supplies continuous loads, or a mix of continuous and noncontinuous loads, the overcurrent device rating may not be less than the noncontinuous load plus 125 percent of the continuous load (unless the assembly with its OCPD is listed for 100 percent operation). The protection itself follows Part I of Article 240.
sections.on_the_job: Match three numbers before energizing: feeder conductor ampacity, breaker rating, and the Article 240 rule you are relying on. If the middle number is larger than the first, name the allowance in the job file.

sections.title: Load calculations — proving the service is big enough
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 220 is the arithmetic of the trade: it turns floor area, appliance nameplates, and heating and cooling equipment into a number that sizes branch circuits, feeders, and services. It offers a standard method that counts loads item by item and, for dwellings, an optional method that uses demand factors on the whole house. Sharma's house services are normally proved with the optional dwelling method, and the app's load calculator is built on it.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 220.1: Article 220 got a new layout built for easier use: seven parts now, with new ones for health care facilities and for marinas and docks. Two new parts: Part VI covers health care facilities, and Part VII covers marinas, boatyards, docks and floating buildings.
• 220.110: New in 2023: patient care spaces get their own demand factor tables for general-purpose receptacle circuits, one for Category 1 and 2 spaces and one for Category 3 and 4. Category 1 and 2 spaces, Table 220.110(1): first 5,000 VA in full, half of the next 5,000 VA, a quarter of the rest.
• 220.5: Garages came off the floor-area exclusion list. In 2023, garage square footage goes into the dwelling's general lighting load, and the rule moved from 220.11 to 220.5(C). An attached garage now counts toward dwelling floor area, so it picks up 3 VA per square foot like the rest of the house (220.41).
• 220.57: New section: each EV charger goes into a feeder or service calc at its nameplate rating, but never less than 7,200 VA. Each piece of electric vehicle supply equipment (EVSE) counts at its nameplate rating or 7,200 VA, whichever is higher.
• 220.60: Air-conditioning loads now get the same 125 percent treatment as motors when you compare noncoincident loads. You still count only the largest of loads that never run together. New: an air-conditioning load in the noncoincident group gets figured at 125 percent, the same as a motor load, when it isn't the largest load.
• 220.70: New section: when an energy management system (EMS) caps the current on a feeder or service, its maximum current setpoint can stand in for the calculated load. If an EMS that meets 750.30 limits a feeder or service, you can use its maximum ampere setpoint as that feeder or service load.
• 220.120: The requirements of Section 555.6 have been moved to 220.120. This will not change the requirements for load calculations or demand factors and is a simple relocation.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

sections.title: General lighting load by floor area
sections.plain_explanation:
In NEC 2020, 220.12 and Table 220.12 set the minimum general lighting load for NON-DWELLING occupancies: the table's unit load (volt-amperes per square foot) times the floor area figured under 220.11 (outside dimensions). The table values already include the 125 percent continuous-load multiplier (table note), so do not apply it again. Dwellings are no longer in this table: the dwelling 3 VA per square foot is 220.14(J).

Table 220.12 unit loads (VA per sq ft):
• Automotive facility — 1.5
• Convention center — 1.4
• Courthouse — 1.4
• Dormitory — 1.5
• Exercise center — 1.4
• Fire station — 1.3
• Gymnasium (armories, auditoriums) — 1.7
• Health care clinic — 1.6
• Hospital — 1.6
• Hotel/motel, incl. apartment houses without tenant cooking (lodge rooms) — 1.7
• Library — 1.5
• Manufacturing facility (industrial commercial lofts) — 2.2
• Motion picture theater — 1.6
• Museum — 1.6
• Office (banks) — 1.3
• Parking garage (commercial storage garages) — 0.3
• Penitentiary — 1.2
• Performing arts theater — 1.5
• Police station — 1.3
• Post office — 1.6
• Religious facility — 2.2
• Restaurant (clubs) — 1.5
• Retail (stores, barber shops, beauty parlors) — 1.9
• School/university — 3
• Sports arena — 3
• Town hall — 1.4
• Transportation — 1.2
• Warehouse — 1.2
• Workshop — 1.7
Office and bank receptacle load is separate: 220.14(K), the larger of 1 VA per sq ft or the 180 VA-per-outlet total after 220.44 demand.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 220.42(A): The non-dwelling unit-load rule moved from 220.12 to 220.42(A) (Table 220.42(A)); the old 220.42 demand factors became 220.45. School/university and sports arena dropped from 3 to 1.5 VA/ft²; all other occupancy values stayed the same. The informational note now assumes 80% power factor.

sections.on_the_job: On a commercial job, pick the occupancy row, multiply by the outside-dimension floor area, and stop there: the 125 percent is already in the number. On a house, use 220.14(J) (3 VA per sq ft), not this table.

sections.title: Other loads — receptacles and named loads at their set values
sections.plain_explanation:
Before any demand factor is applied, this section prices the named loads that are not floor area. The values crews reach for most:
• Receptacle outlets, other than the dwelling general-use receptacles already inside the 3 VA per square foot — 180 VA for each single or multiple receptacle on one yoke or strap
• Multioutlet assemblies — 180 VA for each 5 ft (1.5 m) of assembly where the appliances are unlikely to be used at the same time; 180 VA for each 1 ft where they are likely to be used at the same time where the loads are unlikely to run at the same time, and 180 VA for each 1 ft where they are likely to run together
• Show windows — 200 VA for each linear foot
• A sign or outline lighting circuit — 1,200 VA minimum for each circuit the sign article requires
• Fixed appliances and other named equipment — at nameplate rating, unless another part of Article 220 gives the load its own value or demand table
A duplex receptacle is one yoke and counts once; a single piece of equipment made up of four or more receptacles counts at not less than 90 VA per receptacle (220.14(I)), so a four-plex counts 360 VA.. Motors are sent by this section to the motor rules in Article 430 for their values. Dwelling general-use receptacles are included in the 3 VA per sq ft of 220.14(J) in 2020, not in 220.12.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 220.14(J): 220.14(J) (dwelling 3 VA/ft² lighting and receptacle rule) was deleted from 220.14; the dwelling general lighting load is now 220.41.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: On a commercial tenant build-out, the receptacle count is the load: count straps, not device faces. Worked example: 40 receptacle straps × 180 VA = 7,200 VA of receptacle load before any demand the later sections allow. Write the count on the calc — 'recepts per plan' is not a number an inspector can check.
sections.figure_idea: A duplex receptacle and a four-plex side by side, the duplex tagged 180 VA once and the four-plex tagged 180 VA twice — once per strap.

sections.title: Demand factors for the general load — Table 220.42
sections.plain_explanation:
The standard method does not size a dwelling service for every volt-ampere connected. After the general load is added up (general lighting by floor area, the small-appliance and laundry allowances, and the other general loads), Table 220.42 applies this demand factor to a dwelling:
• First 3,000 VA — at 100 percent
• From 3,001 to 120,000 VA — at 35 percent
• Over 120,000 VA — at 25 percent
The appliance, dryer, and range demands in their own sections are worked separately and added to this result.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 220.45: The Table 220.42 general-lighting demand factors were renumbered as 220.45 / Table 220.45 (the 220.42 number now holds the non-dwelling unit loads).

FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Worked example: a house whose general load adds to 18,000 VA before demand. First 3,000 VA at 100 percent = 3,000 VA. The remaining 15,000 VA at 35 percent = 5,250 VA. Demanded general load = 8,250 VA. Write the two steps down — anyone checking your math wants to see the 3,000 VA block, not just the answer.
sections.figure_idea: Stair-step diagram of Table 220.42: the 100 percent block, the 35 percent block, the 25 percent block, with the worked example filled in.

sections.title: Small-appliance and laundry allowances — 1,500 VA each
sections.plain_explanation:
In the standard method, the kitchen and laundry circuits enter the calculation at set values instead of nameplate numbers:
• Each 20A small-appliance branch circuit — 1,500 VA (a dwelling has at least two, so at least 3,000 VA)
• The laundry branch circuit — 1,500 VA
These allowances are added into the general load first; the Table 220.42 demand factor is then applied to the total. They are calculation allowances only — the circuits themselves are still wired and protected as full 20A circuits.
sections.on_the_job: Worked fragment: two small-appliance circuits (3,000 VA) plus one laundry circuit (1,500 VA) put 4,500 VA into the general load of every standard-method house calculation before floor-area lighting is added. If your worksheet shows less than 4,500 VA on these lines, the sheet is wrong.
sections.figure_idea: Standard-method worksheet with the lines highlighted: small-appliance × 2 = 3,000 VA, laundry = 1,500 VA, feeding into the 220.42 demand step.

sections.title: Four or more fixed appliances — the 75 percent demand
sections.plain_explanation:
In the standard method, a dwelling's fixed appliances almost never all run at once. Where four or more fixed appliances — other than electric ranges, clothes dryers, space-heating equipment, and air-conditioning equipment — are fastened in place on the same service or feeder, this section permits a demand factor of 75 percent on their combined nameplate load:
• Applies at four or more qualifying appliances — three or fewer count at full nameplate
• Demand factor — 75 percent of the combined nameplate ratings
• Never applies to ranges, dryers, heating, or cooling — those have their own sections
Dishwashers, disposals, water heaters, and trash compactors are the usual four that unlock it in a house.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 220.53: EV chargers joined the list of loads kept out of the 75 percent fastened-in-place appliance group. Each one gets figured separately, using 220.57. Electric vehicle supply equipment (EVSE) can't be lumped into the 75 percent appliance group; it's figured on its own (220.57).
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Worked example: dishwasher 1,200 VA + disposal 900 VA + water heater 4,500 VA + trash compactor 1,000 VA = 7,600 VA of nameplate load; × 75 percent = 5,700 VA carried into the service total. Count the appliances on the plan before you decide the factor is unavailable — the fourth appliance is easy to miss.
sections.figure_idea: Four appliance nameplates adding to 7,600 VA, an arrow marked 75 percent, and 5,700 VA landing in the service total.

nec2023_change.change: EV chargers joined the list of loads kept out of the 75 percent fastened-in-place appliance group. Each one gets figured separately, using 220.57. Electric vehicle supply equipment (EVSE) can't be lumped into the 75 percent appliance group; it's figured on its own (220.57).
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 220.53 Dwelling appliance demand factor

sections.title: Clothes dryers — 5,000 VA each and the dryer demand table
sections.plain_explanation:
A household clothes dryer enters the standard-method calculation at 5,000 VA (5 kW) or its nameplate rating, whichever is larger — per dryer. Where several dryers share a service or feeder, Table 220.54 then applies a demand factor to their combined load:
• 1 to 4 dryers — 100 percent
• 5 dryers — 85 percent
• 6 dryers — 75 percent
• 7 dryers — 65 percent
• 8 dryers — 60 percent
• 9 dryers — 55 percent
• 10 dryers — 50 percent
• 11 dryers — 47 percent
The table continues downward for larger counts, which is a multifamily and laundromat case. The portion of the dryer load on the neutral may be taken at 70 percent — see the 220.61 page.
sections.on_the_job: A single house dryer is simple: read the nameplate, and if it says less than 5,000 VA, use 5,000 VA anyway; if it says 5,600 VA, use 5,600 VA. The demand table only starts to matter on the fifth dryer.
sections.figure_idea: A row of dryer nameplates, the first four tagged 100 percent and the fifth tagged 85 percent, showing where the table starts to bite.

sections.title: Household ranges — the Table 220.55 demand values
sections.plain_explanation:
A household range is never counted at full nameplate in a dwelling load calculation — not all of its elements run together for long. Column C gives the demand for ranges not over 12 kW rating; Columns A and B may be used instead for appliances rated 1¾ kW through 8¾ kW (Note 3).:
• 1 range — 8 kW
• 2 ranges — 11 kW
• 3 ranges — 14 kW
• 4 ranges — 17 kW
For a single range rated over 12 kW through 27 kW, start at 8 kW and add 400 VA for each kW — or major fraction of a kW — by which the nameplate exceeds 12 kW. A counter-mounted cooking unit and not more than two wall-mounted ovens, all supplied from one branch circuit and located in the same room, are added together by nameplate and treated as one range (Note 4, branch-circuit load). The portion of the range load on the neutral may be taken at 70 percent — see the 220.61 page. For a range over 12 kW, increase the Column C value 5 percent for each kW or major fraction of a kW over 12 kW (Note 1); for one range that is 400 VA per kW.
sections.on_the_job: Worked example: a 12 kW range counts 8,000 VA in the standard method — not 12,000 VA. A 16 kW range counts 8,000 + (4 × 400) = 9,600 VA. Do not carry this table into the optional method: under 220.82(B) the range goes into the general block at nameplate, and the two methods are never mixed on one calculation.
sections.figure_idea: A range nameplate reading 12 kW, an arrow through Table 220.55 Column C, and 8 kW landing in the load total.

sections.title: The neutral load — and the 70 percent rule
sections.plain_explanation:
The grounded (neutral) conductor of a feeder or service only carries the unbalanced load — the largest load connected between the neutral and any one ungrounded conductor. This section then allows demand on that neutral load:
• The portion of the neutral load from line-to-neutral loads — the first 200A counts at 100 percent, and any portion over 200A counts at 70 percent
• The neutral portion of range and dryer loads may be taken at 70 percent (the range and dryer demand values themselves come from 220.55 and 220.54)
• No reduction is permitted for the neutral of a 4-wire, 3-phase wye system feeding nonlinear loads — discharge lighting, electronic gear, and the like can load a neutral beyond the unbalance, and the 70 percent step does not apply there No reduction is permitted on the neutral of a 3-wire circuit made of two ungrounded conductors and the neutral of a 4-wire, 3-phase wye system (220.61(C)(1)), and none on the portion made of nonlinear loads on a 4-wire, 3-phase wye (220.61(C)(2)). The 70 percent step over 200A applies only to the portion of the unbalanced load in excess of 200 amperes (220.61(B)(2)).
sections.on_the_job: On a large house service the neutral can legitimately come out smaller than the ungrounded conductors — but only by this arithmetic, written into the calculation in the job file. If the calc does not show the 200A step and the 70 percent step, the smaller neutral is an assumption, not a design.
sections.figure_idea: A neutral load bar split at 200A: the first block marked 100 percent, the remainder marked 70 percent, feeding the neutral conductor size.

sections.title: The optional method for a dwelling service or feeder
sections.plain_explanation:
Where a feeder or service supplies an entire dwelling, this optional method lets the load be totaled with demand factors instead of adding every load at full value. The method has conditions: it is for a dwelling, the service or feeder must carry the entire load, and the rating must meet the minimum this section sets. The general-loads part and the heating-and-cooling part are calculated separately and then added, and the existing calc table 220.82 in the app carries the rule rows and worked test cases for the method.

One condition is a floor: the method is available only where the service-entrance conductors have an ampacity of 100A or more — below that, the standard method governs.
sections.on_the_job:
Use the app calculator, then hand-check the two parts before you order gear: the demand-factored general load, and the larger heating-or-cooling figure. Save the printout or worksheet with the permit paperwork.

Worked example — a 1,800 sq ft house. General loads: floor area 1,800 × 3 VA = 5,400 VA; two small-appliance circuits 3,000 VA; laundry circuit 1,500 VA; dishwasher 1,200 VA; disposal 900 VA; water heater 4,500 VA; dryer 5,000 VA; range at nameplate 12,000 VA — total 33,500 VA. The first 10,000 VA counts at 100 percent and the remaining 23,500 VA at 40 percent = 9,400 VA, so the general block is 19,400 VA. Heating and cooling: the air conditioner at 5,760 VA is the largest selection, so add 5,760 VA. Total 25,160 VA ÷ 240 V ≈ 105A — the service is sized at or above that figure.
sections.sharma_note: S-09 affects the gear this calculation sizes: meter and panel back to back where the house allows.
sections.figure_idea: The calculator screen for 220.82 with its two blocks — general loads and heating/cooling — feeding a single service size.

sections.title: Optional method — the general loads
sections.plain_explanation: The general-loads block starts with floor area at 3 VA per square foot, adds 1,500 VA for each small-appliance circuit and for the laundry circuit, and adds the nameplate ratings of the appliances and motors the subsection lists. The first 10 kVA of that total is taken at full value and the remainder at 40 percent. That demand step is the whole advantage of the optional method, and it only applies to the loads this block covers — heating and cooling are handled separately in the next part.
sections.on_the_job: Count circuits, not appliances, for the 1,500 VA blocks: two small-appliance circuits are required, and a third one that is installed also counts. Use nameplate VA where a rating is given in amps and volts.
sections.figure_idea: A bar showing a general-load total split at 10 kVA: the first block at 100 percent, the rest at 40 percent.

sections.title: Optional method — heating and cooling
sections.plain_explanation: Heating and cooling do not run at full load together, so this part adds only the largest of six selections, in kVA: (1) air conditioning and cooling at 100 percent of nameplate; (2) a heat pump with no supplemental electric heat, at 100 percent; (3) a heat pump at 100 percent of the compressor plus 65 percent of the supplemental electric heat — the compressor is omitted if it is prevented from running at the same time as that heat; (4) electric space heating at 65 percent with fewer than four separately controlled units; (5) electric space heating at 40 percent with four or more separately controlled units; and (6) electric thermal storage and other heating expected to run continuously at full nameplate, at 100 percent — a system counted under (6) is not counted again under another selection.
sections.on_the_job: In Florida the air-conditioning figure usually wins this comparison, but a house with strip heat or a heat pump with auxiliary heat still needs the comparison done and written down. Take the compressor and air-handler figures from nameplates, not from tonnage rules of thumb.
sections.figure_idea: A balance graphic: AC load on one side, heating load on the other, with only the heavier side carried into the total.
sections.florida_note: Florida heat pumps with electric auxiliary heat are common in Sharma's territory; that is the (C)(3) case — compressor at 100 percent plus 65 percent of the auxiliary heat — so do not skip the comparison on a Florida house.

sections.title: Existing dwellings — adding load without changing the service
sections.plain_explanation:
This is the optional method for additions to an existing one-family dwelling: it answers whether the existing service can carry new load, without rebuilding the calculation from zero. The existing load is figured from the values this section lists: 3 VA per square foot for general lighting, 1,500 VA per small-appliance and laundry circuit, and nameplate ratings of appliances. (Figuring an existing load from actual loads or demand data is 220.87, not this section.) Then:
• Where the added load is other than air conditioning or electric space heating — combine the existing load and the added load, take the first 8 kVA at 100 percent and the remainder at 40 percent; if that result does not exceed the existing service rating, no service increase is required
• Where air conditioning or space heating is added (220.83(B)) — air-conditioning equipment at 100 percent; central electric space heating at 100 percent; fewer than four separately controlled space-heating units at 100 percent; the first 8 kVA of all other loads at 100 percent; the remainder of all other loads at 40 percent
If the result exceeds the existing service rating, the service is increased and sized under the regular methods.
sections.on_the_job: Worked example: an existing 200A service carries a computed existing load of 26 kVA, and the owner adds a 6 kVA workshop load. Combined 32 kVA: first 8 kVA at 100 percent, remaining 24 kVA at 40 percent = 9.6 kVA — total 17.6 kVA, or about 73A at 240V, well under the 200A service. No service change. Keep this worksheet with the permit — it is the document that proves the existing service was checked, not assumed.
sections.figure_idea: An existing panel with its load total, a new load added beside it, the 8 kVA / 40 percent split applied, and the result compared against the existing service rating.

sections.title: Outside branch circuits and feeders
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 225 covers wiring that runs outside — between buildings, across a yard, or overhead or underground to a detached structure. Its recurring themes are clearances, support, a disconnect at the building being supplied, and limits on how many supplies a building may have. Sharma meets it on detached garages, barns, pool houses, and site lighting fed from a house or a main building.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 225.41 / 225.42 / 225.5 / 225.7: New 225.41: an outdoor emergency disconnect is required for one- and two-family dwellings supplied by a feeder (mirrors 230.85). New 225.42: SPD on feeders supplying dwelling-type occupancies. 225.5 (size of conductors) and 225.7 (lighting equipment on poles) were deleted.
• 225.27: Raceways coming into a building from outside still get sealed. New in 2023, the rule says how: the seal has to meet both 300.5(G) and 300.7(A). The seal now has to satisfy 300.5(G), the underground raceway seal rule, and 300.7(A), the rule for raceways passing from warm to cold.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: When a run leaves a building, switch articles. A feeder inside one building and the same feeder continued to a second building are judged by different pages, and the second building needs its own disconnect and grounding treatment.
sections.figure_idea: A site plan: house panel, a buried feeder crossing a yard, and a detached garage with its own disconnect and ground rods.
