sections.title: Clearances for outside overhead conductors
sections.plain_explanation:
Conductors run overhead outside — a feeder across a yard to a detached garage is Sharma's common case — must clear what is under and beside them. The vertical clearances from this section, measured at the conductor's lowest point:
• Over roofs — not a 225.18 item: roof clearance is 225.19(A), 8 ft 6 in., with the reductions listed there
• Over areas subject only to pedestrian traffic — 10 ft
• Over residential driveways and other residential property — 12 ft
• Over other land traversed by vehicles, such as cultivated or grazing land — 15 ft
• Over roads, streets, alleys, parking lots, and areas subject to truck traffic — 18 ft
Clearance is judged at final sag, not at the height the conductor left the pole or mast on a cool morning.
sections.on_the_job: Walk the span before you set the attachment heights: the same garage feeder is a 10 ft job over the lawn, a 12 ft job where it crosses the driveway, and an 18 ft job if it crosses the street. The highest number on the route sets the attachment.
sections.figure_idea: A yard feeder span in profile crossing lawn, driveway, and street edge, with 10 ft, 12 ft, and 18 ft clearance lines drawn under it.

sections.title: How many supplies may feed one building
sections.plain_explanation: The general rule is one: a building or structure gets a single feeder or branch circuit, or a single set of feeders, subject to the exceptions the section lists for things such as emergency and standby systems, fire pumps, and certain large or separately controlled installations. Two ordinary feeders run to the same detached garage because two panels were convenient is not one of the ordinary cases. Where an exception is used, the building must carry a permanent plaque or directory showing where the other disconnects are.
sections.on_the_job: Before running a second supply to a structure that already has one, name the exception in writing in the job file. If you cannot name one, redesign to a single larger feeder and a subpanel.

sections.title: A disconnect at the building being supplied
sections.plain_explanation:
A feeder or branch circuit supplying another building must have a disconnecting means at that building, located and grouped as this section and the following sections require, suitable for use as service equipment where required, and rated as those sections set out. The disconnect is what lets a person at the detached building kill its power without walking back to the main building. Its rating and location rules sit in the sections immediately after this one, so read them together on a real job.

How many disconnects there may be, and how they are marked, sit in the sections right after this one:
• The building's supply may be disconnected by up to six switches or circuit breakers, in a single enclosure or a group of separate enclosures (225.33)
• The disconnects are grouped together, and each one is marked to show exactly what it disconnects (225.34)
• A feeder disconnecting means serving a one-family dwelling is rated at least 100 amperes (225.39(D)) The one-family dwelling 100A rating is 225.39(C); 225.39(D) is 'All Others' at 60A. The disconnect must open all ungrounded conductors that supply or pass through the building (225.31), and it must be suitable for use as service equipment only where applied under 250.32(B)(1) Exception No. 1 (225.36).
sections.on_the_job:
Mount and label the disconnect at rough-in, not at final. If the feeder feeds a subpanel inside the building, confirm which device is the building disconnect and that it is grouped and marked as such.

Count the disconnects before you set the gear: if the design needs a seventh throw, the design changes — one larger disconnecting means or a single main — not a seventh handle in a second can across the room.

sections.title: Where the separate building's disconnect must be
sections.plain_explanation: The disconnecting means for a feeder or branch circuit supplying a separate building goes in a readily accessible location either outside the building or inside, nearest the point where the conductors enter. 'Nearest the point of entrance' is the load-bearing phrase: feeder conductors inside the building are ahead of the building's own disconnect until they reach it, so the run from the entry point to the disconnect is kept as short as the building allows. Exceptions cover large multibuilding industrial or institutional sites under single management with documented safe switching, and poles or towers used as lighting standards, among others; read the listed exceptions in the printed text before relying on one. Fire pumps are an additional-supply permission under 225.30, not a 225.32 location exception. For this section, the 230.6 rules decide when conductors are considered outside the building.
sections.on_the_job: On a detached garage or casita, plan the panel or disconnect at the wall where the feeder enters — not across the building because the layout was prettier. If the feeder enters underground on the far side from the planned panel, that is a redesign conversation before the trench, not after.

sections.title: Services — where utility power enters
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 230 governs the service: the conductors and equipment that bring utility power to the building and end at the service disconnect. It covers how many services a building may have, conductor clearances, where the disconnect goes and how many there may be, how big a dwelling service must be, and two 2020 additions Sharma sees on every house — surge protection and an outdoor emergency disconnect. The meter and panel layout a builder notices most is decided here and in Article 250.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 230.30: Type TC-ER cable can now carry underground service conductors, but only when the cable is identified for both direct burial and service-entrance use. Underground service conductors can now run in Type TC-ER cable (230.30(B)).
• 230.43: Type TC-ER cable still works for service-entrance conductors, but only cable identified for service-entrance use counts now. Ordinary TC-ER, allowed in 2020, no longer qualifies. Only TC-ER that carries a service-entrance identification can be used for service-entrance conductors (230.43(20)).
• 230.62: The barrier rule in service equipment now plainly covers the parts that stay energized with the service disconnect open, so a worker on the load side can't brush live line terminals. Barriers have to guard energized, uninsulated, ungrounded busbars and terminals while the service disconnect is open (230.62(C)).
• 230.7: Underground boxes and handhole enclosures joined the list. Other conductors can't share a service raceway, service cable, underground box or handhole with the service conductors. Feeders and branch circuits can't ride in the same underground box or handhole enclosure as the service conductors.
• 230.75: The section of a multi-section switchboard or switchgear lineup that holds the neutral disconnect has to be marked again. The 2020 edition had left that marking rule out. Multi-section switchboards and switchgear can put the neutral disconnect in any one section, and that section now has to be marked.
• 230.8: Underground service raceways entering a building still get sealed, and in 2023 the seal also has to meet 300.7(A) for temperature differences, not just 300.5(G). The seal now has to satisfy 300.7(A) too, which targets warm air moving into a cold section of raceway and condensing.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Plan the service as one assembly at rough-in: drop or lateral clearances, meter position, disconnect, SPD, emergency disconnect, grounding electrode system. Finding one piece missing at final is a re-inspection.
sections.sharma_note: S-09: meter outside, panel inside directly behind it, where the house allows. S-02: new service gear is Siemens.

sections.title: Clearances for service conductors
sections.plain_explanation:
Service conductors that run where people, windows, doors, and vehicles can reach them need clearance. Overhead conductors near a building must keep the distances this section sets from windows, doors, porches, and similar features, with a stated allowance where conductors run above an opening. Underground and other service arrangements are handled by their own parts of the article and by Article 300 burial rules.

The building-opening number in this section:
• Service conductors must be kept at least 3 ft from windows that are designed to be opened, doors, porches, balconies, fire escapes, and similar features
• Conductors run above the top level of a window are the stated exception to that 3 ft clearance
The vertical clearances — how high the conductors must run over roofs, yards, driveways, and streets — are a separate set of numbers in 230.24, covered on its own page. The 3 ft clearance applies to service conductors installed as open conductors or as multiconductor cable without an overall outer jacket. Jacketed SE cable is not subject to the 3 ft rule. 230.9(B): conductors above platforms and similar areas need the 10 ft vertical clearance of 230.24(B). 230.9(C): overhead service conductors may not be installed beneath openings through which materials may be moved, and may not obstruct those openings.
sections.on_the_job: Check the drop against the finished building, not the framing: a window that will open, a porch roof, and a balcony added on a plan revision all change the clearance picture. Use the existing lookup item for the window rule crews ask about most.
sections.florida_note: The utility's own service standards also apply in Florida and may be stricter at the pole and weatherhead; the AHJ and the serving utility both have a say at the service.

sections.title: Overhead service conductors — clearance heights
sections.plain_explanation:
These are the heights an overhead service drop or overhead service conductors must keep, measured to the lowest point of the span, including the drip loop:
• Above a roof — 8 ft, and that clearance must be kept for at least 3 ft in all directions from the edge of the roof
• Above a roof with a slope of 4 in 12 or steeper, where the voltage between conductors does not exceed 300V — 3 ft is permitted
• Over a roof overhang only — as low as 18 in, where not more than 6 ft of conductor passes over not more than 4 ft of overhang and the conductors terminate in a through-the-roof raceway or approved support (the mast case)
• Above areas subject only to pedestrian traffic — 10 ft
• Above residential property and driveways — 12 ft
• Above roads, streets, alleys, and commercial areas subject to truck traffic, including commercial driveways and parking lots — 18 ft
The mast and attachment are built to whichever of these numbers the span actually crosses — the utility's own service standards may require more. 10 ft — at the service entrance, at the lowest point of the drip loop, and over pedestrian-only areas, only for conductors supported on and cabled with a grounded bare messenger and not over 150V to ground; 12 ft — residential property and driveways, and commercial areas not subject to truck traffic, not over 300V to ground; 15 ft — those 12-ft areas where the voltage exceeds 300V to ground; 18 ft — public streets, alleys, roads, parking areas subject to truck traffic, driveways on other than residential property, and other land traversed by vehicles (cultivated, grazing, forest, orchard); 24.5 ft — over track rails. Exception No. 4: the 3 ft-beyond-the-edge requirement does not apply to the final span attached to the side of the building. Exception No. 5: 3 ft is permitted where the voltage between conductors does not exceed 300V and the roof area is guarded or isolated.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 230.24: Service conductors running over a roof must now clear it by 8 ft 6 in, not 8 ft. Overhead feeders already used that number. The minimum height from the roof surface up to overhead service conductors is now 8 ft 6 in instead of 8 ft (230.24(A)).
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Set the mast height from the span, not from habit: measure the route, find the highest clearance it crosses, add sag, and that is the weatherhead height. A drop that clears the roof by 8 ft but sags to 11 ft over the driveway fails the driveway number.

sections.title: Service masts — what may ride on the mast
sections.plain_explanation: Where a mast is used to support overhead service conductors, the mast itself is part of the service. Only power service-drop or overhead service conductors may be attached to it — no other conductors, and no antennas or other equipment that is not part of the service. The mast has to be strong enough for the strain the utility's drop puts on it, or be braced or guyed, and the fittings where conductors pass through or terminate are listed service fittings (the weatherhead and drip loop are on the 230.54 page). A mast that also carries a yard-light feed or a cable TV drop is a violation you can see from the street. 230.28(A): hubs used with a conduit service mast must be identified for use with service-entrance equipment. 230.28(B): service-drop or overhead service conductors may not be attached to the mast between the weatherhead (or end of the conduit) and a coupling where the coupling is above the last conduit support or above the building.
sections.on_the_job: Check the mast before the utility arrives: listed weatherhead, hub wrench-tight, guys where the span is long, and nothing else clamped to the pipe. Confirm the utility's attachment requirements at rough-in — masts through or over the roof carry height and bracing rules in the serving utility's standards as well.
sections.figure_idea: Service mast elevation: weatherhead, drip loop, and guys, with a red X over a TV antenna and a yard-light cable clamped to the same mast.
sections.florida_note: Florida utilities publish their own service standards (attachment heights, mast specifications, meter positions). The NEC sets the floor; the serving utility's book can add to it, and the utility connects last — build to both.

sections.title: Minimum size and rating of service-entrance conductors
sections.plain_explanation: Service-entrance conductors are sized for the calculated load from Article 220 — the calculation, not the size of the panel that was ordered, sets the floor. The conductor ampacity has to carry the load and coordinate with the service overcurrent protection; for a one-family dwelling the service itself may not be smaller than 100A (that rating rule is on the 230.79(C) page), and dwelling services and whole-load feeders may use the 83 percent sizing rule covered in Chapter 3 at 310.12. A 200A panel fed by conductors sized for 100A of calculated load is not a 200A service.
sections.on_the_job: Do the Article 220 math before the service gear is ordered, and keep the worksheet in the job file. If the calculated load lands close to the next standard size, that is a conversation for the office — not a field decision to round the conductors down.
sections.figure_idea: Flow line: Article 220 load → conductor ampacity (or 310.12 for a dwelling) → service disconnect rating → panel, with 'panel size alone' crossed out as a starting point.

sections.title: Overhead service connections — attachment and drip loop
sections.plain_explanation: Where an overhead drop lands, three things have to be right at the top of the service. The point of attachment is located so the clearances on the 230.24 and 230.9 pages can actually be met, and the service head (weatherhead) sits at or above the point of attachment wherever practicable, so water runs away from the raceway instead of into it. The conductors form a drip loop below the weatherhead: each conductor loops down and back up, so rain drips off the bottom of the loop instead of following the wire into the head. Service heads must have conductors of different potential brought out through separately bushed openings (230.54(E))., and splices in service conductors are made only by the methods 230.46 allows. Where it is impracticable to put the service head above the point of attachment, it must be within 24 in. of the point of attachment (230.54(C) exception). Drip loops and service-entrance conductors must be arranged so water will not enter the raceway or equipment (230.54(F), (G)).
sections.on_the_job: Form the drip loop long enough to actually drip — a tight little kink at the head is not a loop. Leave the utility the working tails at the length its standards call for, and do not tape or splice anything at the weatherhead that the utility will have to undo.
sections.figure_idea: Weatherhead detail: attachment point, head above it, drip loop hanging below with a droplet falling from the bottom of the loop.
sections.florida_note: The serving Florida utility's standards set the tail length it wants at the weatherhead and the attachment hardware it accepts; confirm both before the drop is scheduled.

sections.title: Surge protection on the service
sections.plain_explanation:
New in the 2020 edition, this section requires surge protection when a service supplies a dwelling: a listed Type 1 or Type 2 surge protective device, installed in or next to the service equipment, with the rating and connection rules the section states. It also applies when service equipment is replaced. It protects the house's electronics against surges arriving on the service; it is not lightning protection and it is not a substitute for equipment-level protection on sensitive gear.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 215.18 / 225.42 / 242.2: SPD rule spread to feeders: new 215.18 and 225.42 require a Type 1 or Type 2 SPD (10 kA In minimum) where a feeder supplies a dwelling unit, dormitory unit, hotel/motel guest room or nursing-home sleeping area. Article 242 itself is not new in 2023 (it was new in 2020); 2023 adds 242.2 (SPDs and surge arresters may not be reconditioned).
• 230.67: Surge protection at the service now reaches dorm units, hotel and motel guest suites and rooms, and nursing home patient sleeping areas. The device itself now needs a 10 kA minimum nominal discharge current rating. Dorm units and the guest rooms and suites of hotels and motels joined dwelling units: their services now need a surge-protective device (SPD).
• 242.9: Starting in 2023, every surge-protective device (SPD) has to show whether it is still working, so anyone can tell when the protection is gone. Every SPD now needs a way to show it is working properly (242.9).
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Confirm the SPD is on the material list for every new house service and every service change, and that its location — integral to the panel or in an enclosure next to it — is drawn before rough-in. A surge device left in the truck is a failed item.

sections.title: Where the service disconnect goes
sections.plain_explanation: The service disconnect must be readily accessible and in one of the locations this section allows: outside the building, or inside near the point where the service conductors enter, subject to the 2020 wording and to what the AHJ accepts for conductor length inside. Every occupant also needs access to disconnecting means for their own space in the occupancies the section covers. The disconnect is what everything downstream is judged from — it is where the service ends and feeders and branch circuits begin.
sections.on_the_job: Decide the disconnect location with the inspector's local practice in mind before the service is built, especially on a service change where an older inside location is being reused. Keep the path to it clear and the location marked.
sections.sharma_note: S-09's back-to-back layout puts the panel directly behind the meter, which keeps service conductors inside the building to the shortest practical run.
sections.florida_note: Florida AHJs differ on how much service conductor they accept inside a building before the disconnect. Confirm the local position on a service layout that is not the standard back-to-back arrangement.

sections.title: How many service disconnects, and how they are grouped
sections.plain_explanation:
The 2020 edition reorganized this rule: a service may have two to six disconnecting means, and 230.71(B) permits four arrangements — (1) separate enclosures for each disconnect; (2) panelboards, each with its own main disconnect; (3) a switchboard with each disconnect in a separate barriered vertical section; or (4) switchgear or metering centers with each disconnect in its own compartment. The disconnects must be grouped as 230.71(A) requires. A single multi-switch assembly is not automatically wrong — it counts where it fits one of these four arrangements.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 230.71: Transfer switches and motor control centers joined the two-to-six disconnect list, separate meter centers got their own item, and older equipment that legally grouped service disconnects in one enclosure gets a pass. New exception: existing service equipment built under an older edition that allowed grouped disconnects can keep up to six in one enclosure, section or compartment.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: On a service with more than one disconnect, show the arrangement on the plan — separate enclosures, panelboards with mains, barriered switchboard sections, or compartmented switchgear — and show the grouping. Do not condemn a compliant panelboard or switchboard service for not having separate enclosures.

sections.title: Minimum size for a one-family dwelling service
sections.plain_explanation: A one-family dwelling service disconnect is rated at least 100 amperes, 3-wire. That is a floor, not a recommendation: the Article 220 calculation governs whenever it comes out higher, which on a modern Florida house with electric range, dryer, water heating, and air conditioning it usually does. Other occupancies and uses have their own minimums in the surrounding subsections of 230.79.
sections.on_the_job: Never quote a 100A service because it is the minimum. Run the calculation, and if the result is close to a standard size, say so with the worksheet in hand.

sections.title: What may connect ahead of the service disconnect
sections.plain_explanation: The line side of the service disconnect is a closed list. The equipment this section allows to connect on the supply side includes meter enclosures and meter disconnect switches, current-transformer cabinets, Type 1 surge-protective devices (and surge arresters) are permitted on the supply side; the 230.67 dwelling SPD may be installed on the line or load side, and is usually a Type 1 or Type 2 at the service equipment., taps used only to supply load-management devices, circuits for standby power systems, fire pump equipment, and fire and sprinkler alarms, if provided with service equipment and installed as service-entrance conductors. made under their own articles, and supply-side interconnections such as a solar system connected ahead of the main under Article 705's rules. Anything not on the list waits for the load side. Conductors ahead of the disconnect have no building overcurrent protection of their own, which is why the list stays short. Cable limiters are also permitted on the supply side. A meter disconnect needs a short-circuit current rating at least equal to the available fault current, must be able to interrupt the load served, and must be field-marked 'METER DISCONNECT – NOT SERVICE EQUIPMENT'. Article 705 supply-side sources need a disconnect suitable for use as service equipment plus overcurrent protection per Part VII.
sections.on_the_job: Solar supply-side taps are the live case on Sharma roofs: the tap hardware, its rating, and where it lands are engineered decisions made before rough-in, with the utility and the AHJ in the loop — never a field improvisation inside a meter can.

sections.title: An outdoor emergency disconnect for dwellings
sections.plain_explanation:
Also new in 2020, this section requires one- and two-family dwellings to have an emergency disconnect in a readily accessible outdoor location, marked as the emergency disconnect in the way the section requires. It exists so firefighters and first responders can kill power to the house without entering it. Where the service equipment itself is outdoors and meets the section, the arrangement may already satisfy it; where the disconnect is indoors, a separate outdoor device is the usual answer.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 230.85: The dwelling emergency disconnect rule got tighter: replacing service equipment now triggers it, other power sources need a location sign, and labels go white on red with 1/2 in letters. Replacing the service equipment on a one- or two-family home now brings the emergency disconnect requirement with it (230.85(C)).
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Add the emergency disconnect to the service material list and the plan notes at the same time as the SPD — the two 2020 items are missed together. Mark it as required, not with a generic label.
sections.sharma_note: S-02: the device is part of the Siemens service gear package on a new Sharma service.

sections.title: Overcurrent protection — breakers and fuses
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 240 is the protection article: it decides where overcurrent devices go, what standard ratings exist, how conductors are protected, when the next higher rating may be used, how tap conductors work, and where panels may and may not be located. A breaker has two jobs that must not be confused — it protects the conductor, and only through that does it protect the equipment and the building. Most of Article 240 that Sharma uses daily is in 240.4 and 240.24.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 240.11: When a rule makes one feeder's overcurrent device selectively coordinate with the service device, every other feeder fed directly from that service device now has to coordinate with it too. Once one feeder device must selectively coordinate with the service device, every feeder device fed straight from that service device must coordinate with it (240.11).
• 240.16: Branch-circuit breakers and fuses still need at least 5,000 amps of interrupting rating, but that floor moved out of the Article 100 definition and into new 240.16. Any breaker or fuse doing branch-circuit duty must be rated to interrupt 5,000 amps or more (240.16).
• 240.60: New in 2023: a fuse reducer, the adapter that lets a smaller fuse sit in clips made for a bigger one, has to be a listed product. Every fuse reducer now has to be listed. A shop-made spacer or an adapter with no listing mark doesn't pass.
• 240.7: Three kinds of protective devices now have to be listed: branch-circuit breakers and fuses, the relays and breakers that provide ground-fault protection of equipment, and GFCIs. Branch-circuit rated breakers and fuses, the kind that can protect services, feeders and branch circuits, have to be listed. Supplementary protectors aren't on this list.
• 240.89: New in 2023: a replacement trip unit has to carry a listing for use in the specific circuit breaker it goes into. Fitting the frame isn't enough. Swapping a breaker's trip unit? The new unit needs a listing that covers that particular breaker, not just a matching shape.
• 240.2: The reconditioning requirements located at 240.62 and 240.88 were relocated to Section 240.2 in the 2023 NEC. Ground-fault protection of equipment (GFPE) and ground-fault circuit interrupters (GFCI) were added to the list of equipment that shall not be reconditioned.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

sections.title: Protecting a conductor at its ampacity
sections.plain_explanation:
The starting rule of the article is simple: conductors are protected against overcurrent at their ampacity, in the ways this section then refines. It points to the special cases handled elsewhere — motors, air conditioning, welders, transformers, and others — where the nameplate or a specific article changes the protection picture. It also contains the two allowances Sharma uses most, covered on the next two pages: rounding up to the next standard rating in limited conditions, and the small-conductor caps.

New 240.4(H): a dwelling service or feeder sized with 310.12 can be protected at that full rating, like a 200-amp breaker on 2/0 copper.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: When equipment has a nameplate that states its own maximum protection, follow that equipment article and the nameplate — the general rule here is not permission to upsize. Write the special-case citation in the job file when you use one.

sections.title: When the next higher breaker size may be used
sections.plain_explanation:
Where a conductor's ampacity does not land on a standard rating, the next higher standard overcurrent device may be used only when the conditions in this subsection are all met. It is an allowance with fences, not a general right to round up. The existing lookup item works the common examples.

The three conditions:
• (1) The conductors are not part of a branch circuit supplying more than one receptacle for cord-and-plug-connected portable loads
• (2) The conductor ampacity does not correspond to a standard fuse or circuit-breaker rating (breakers without overload-trip adjustment above their rating)
• (3) The next higher standard rating selected does not exceed 800A
There is no separate 'ampacity does not exceed 800A' test in the rule. Past 800A there is no rounding up: under 240.4(C) the conductor ampacity must be at least equal to the device rating.

• 240.4(B): Added adjustable trip overcurrent protective devices as being permitted to have an ampacity value set that does not exceed the next higher standard overcurrent protection device ampacity value [per Table 240.6(A)] above the ampacity of the conductors being protected.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: State all three conditions when you use this allowance on a feeder or an equipment circuit. If the circuit feeds receptacles on a multi-outlet branch circuit, stop — the allowance is not available.

sections.title: The small-conductor caps
sections.plain_explanation:
Whatever the ampacity table allows at a higher temperature rating, this subsection caps overcurrent protection for small conductors: 14 AWG copper at 15A, 12 AWG copper at 20A, and 10 AWG copper at 30A, with tighter caps for aluminum and copper-clad aluminum — 12 AWG at 15A and 10 AWG at 25A. Specific equipment articles can direct otherwise for their own equipment, but for general branch wiring these caps are the numbers that decide the breaker. They are also why a 12 AWG conductor on a 25A breaker fails inspection even when a table column seems to allow the ampacity.

sections.title: Standard ratings for breakers and fuses
sections.plain_explanation:
Overcurrent devices come in standard ampere ratings, and this section lists them — the familiar steps from small branch ratings through the large service ratings, plus the additional standard ratings it names for fuses. Nonstandard ratings exist only in the limited cases the Code allows. A calculation that lands between two standard ratings is resolved by the protection rules, not by ordering a breaker in the calculated size.

The standard ratings (240.6(A)):
• 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90, 100
• 110, 125, 150, 175, 200, 225, 250, 300, 350, 400, 450, 500, 600
• 700, 800, 1000, 1200, 1600, 2000, 2500, 3000, 4000, 5000, 6000
Fuses also have additional standard ratings of 1, 3, 6, 10, and 601 amperes. Note the gaps crews trip on: there is no standard 105A, 130A, or 275A device — a calculation landing there resolves to a standard rating under the protection rules.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 240.6: Ten amps moved into the standard ratings table, so 10-amp breakers are now standard along with fuses. New 240.6(D) covers breakers whose trip setting can be changed remotely. Table 240.6(A) now starts at 10 amps, making 10 a standard size for inverse-time breakers as well as fuses.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: When a load calculation lands at a nonstandard number, write the next step as a choice between the standard ratings on either side and record which rule you used. Do not write a nonstandard breaker size on a material list.

sections.title: Feeder taps — the 10 ft and 25 ft rules
sections.plain_explanation:
A tap is a conductor that leaves a feeder without its own overcurrent protection at the point of supply, protected instead by the feeder's larger device. That is permitted only inside the fences of this section. The two rules used most:
• The 10 ft tap — tap conductors not over 10 ft long, with ampacity not less than the combined calculated loads and not less than the rating of the equipment, or of the overcurrent device, the tap supplies; the conductors do not extend beyond the panelboard, switchboard or device they supply; they are enclosed in a raceway (except at the termination) and protected from physical damage; and, for field installations where the tap leaves the enclosure or vault it is made in, ampacity not less than one-tenth of the feeder OCPD rating
• The 25 ft tap — tap conductors not over 25 ft long, with ampacity not less than one-third the rating of the feeder's overcurrent device, terminating in a single circuit breaker or single set of fuses that limits the load to the tap ampacity, with the conductors protected from physical damage
Longer taps, outside taps, and transformer taps have their own conditions in this section — a tap that fits neither rule above is not made legal by being short-ish.
sections.on_the_job: Worked example: tapping a 400A feeder to feed a 100A panelboard nearby. As a 10 ft tap, the conductors need ampacity of at least 100A (the device supplied) — comfortably over one-tenth of 400A. As a 25 ft tap they would need at least one-third of 400A, about 133A — the longer tap demands the bigger wire. Measure the actual run before choosing which rule you are on.
sections.figure_idea: A 400A feeder with two taps drawn: a short tap tagged 10 ft rule / one-tenth, and a longer tap tagged 25 ft rule / one-third, each ending in its own breaker.

sections.title: Where overcurrent devices may be located
sections.plain_explanation:
Circuit breakers and switches containing fuses must be readily accessible and installed so the center of the grip of the operating handle, at its highest position, is not more than 6 ft 7 in above the floor or working platform. That height limit does not apply in four cases: busways, under 368.17(C); supplementary overcurrent protection, under 240.10; overcurrent devices described in 225.40 and 230.92; and devices next to the utilization equipment they supply, where access may be by portable means. A tool may be used to reach devices inside listed industrial control panels or similar enclosures. The rest of this section bars devices near easily ignitable material and in clothes closets, and, in dwellings, in bathrooms.

No breakers or fuses in a bathroom, a shower facility, or a locker room that has showers, whether it's a house, gym or factory (240.24(E)).
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Measure handle height to the top breaker in the panel as installed, including a raised floor or platform change on a remodel. And site the panel early: a closet or bathroom location is a relocation, not a waiver request.

sections.title: Breaker markings — and the slash-rating trap
sections.plain_explanation: A circuit breaker's markings are working information: ampere rating and voltage rating are marked by the manufacturer, the interrupting rating is marked on breakers with an interrupting rating other than 5,000A (240.83(C))., and special-duty markings tell you where the breaker may be applied — SWD for breakers used to switch fluorescent or HID lighting loads, HACR for heating, air-conditioning and refrigeration equipment. Voltage markings come in two forms. A straight-rated breaker (e.g., 240V) may be applied where the nominal voltage between any two conductors does not exceed its rating. A slash-rated breaker (120/240V, 480Y/277V) may be applied only in a solidly grounded circuit where no conductor's nominal voltage to ground exceeds the lower value and the voltage between any two conductors does not exceed the higher value — which is why a slash-rated breaker does not belong on the high leg of a 240V delta system (208V to ground) or on a corner-grounded system.
sections.on_the_job: On a high-leg delta panel, read the breaker voltage marking before you land the high leg: a 120/240 slash-rated breaker is the wrong breaker there even though the amp rating matches. Check the marking on the breaker in your hand, not the one you expected to find in the box.
sections.sharma_note: S-02: new gear is Siemens. The marking check applies to whatever breaker is actually installed — a substituted breaker with the wrong voltage rating is still the wrong breaker.
sections.figure_idea: Two breaker labels side by side: a '240V' straight rating approved for the high leg, a '120/240V' slash rating crossed out for the high leg, with the SWD and HACR marks called out.

sections.title: Grounding and bonding — the fault-current path
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 250 is the longest and most argued article in this chapter. Grounding connects a system to earth through electrodes; bonding connects metal parts together so a fault has a low-impedance path back to the source that trips the breaker fast. Earth itself is not that fault path — the breaker trips because bonding carries the fault home. The pages that follow walk the service bond, the electrodes, the sizing tables, and the piping and intersystem bonds in that order.

• 250.100: The hazardous-location bonding rule was reworded for accuracy. Raceways, metal-clad cable, equipment and enclosures still need threaded, threadless or listed bonding fittings, even with a wire-type equipment grounding conductor (EGC). In classified locations, bond with a method from 250.92(B)(2) through (B)(4): wrenchtight threaded entries, tight threadless fittings, or other listed bonding devices.
• 250.109: Plaster rings and extension rings now join metal covers and fittings: each must be fastened to a metal box so the fault path holds, or bonded with a jumper or equipment grounding conductor (EGC). Metal covers, plaster rings, extension rings and metal fittings must be fastened so the fault path holds, or else bonded with a jumper or EGC.
• 250.114: Cord-and-plug ice makers joined the list of appliances whose exposed metal parts must connect to an equipment grounding conductor (EGC), in homes and other occupancies alike. Ice makers now sit next to refrigerators, freezers and air conditioners in the residential list, 250.114(3).
• 250.130: 250.130(C) now covers swapping out a nongrounding snap switch. An equipment grounding conductor (EGC) added for the new switch can land at the same points already allowed for receptacles. sections.title: What grounding and bonding must accomplish
sections.plain_explanation: This general section states the performance the rest of the article builds: grounded systems are connected to earth in a way that limits voltage from lightning and surges and stabilizes voltage to ground, and electrical equipment and enclosures are bonded together into a continuous, low-impedance path that can carry fault current long enough for the overcurrent device to open. It also states plainly that the earth is not to be used as the sole equipment grounding conductor. When a specific installation rule is unclear, this section is the test it has to pass.
sections.on_the_job: Use this page when a field argument starts: 'will it trip the breaker, fast, every time?' is the question this section asks. If the honest answer is no, the detail is wrong whatever it looks like.

sections.title: How grounding and bonding connections are made
sections.plain_explanation: Grounding and bonding connections are made only by the methods 250.8(A) lists: listed pressure connectors; terminal bars; pressure connectors listed as grounding and bonding equipment; exothermic welding; machine-screw fasteners that engage at least two threads or are secured with a nut; thread-forming machine screws that engage at least two threads in the enclosure; connections that are part of a listed assembly; or other listed means. Connections to an electrode itself follow 250.70 — listed lugs, pressure connectors or clamps, or exothermic welding. Solder alone is never the connection — a soldered-only joint can melt open during a fault, which is the exact moment the path is needed. One screw or terminal takes one conductor unless the device is listed and identified for more.
sections.on_the_job: Crimp, clamp, or weld it — never solder-only. On a service call, two grounds landed under one ordinary green screw and a soldered splice in the grounding path are both rework items: correct them with listed connectors while the panel is open.
sections.figure_idea: Connection lineup: listed pressure connector, exothermic weld, and two-thread machine screw marked approved; a solder-only joint crossed out.

sections.title: Which AC systems must be grounded
sections.plain_explanation: Some AC systems are required to be grounded, and the common Florida systems are on the list: a system that can be grounded so the maximum voltage to ground stays at or below 150 volts must be grounded, and systems whose neutral is used as a circuit conductor — the 120/240V house service, 208Y/120V and 480Y/277V commercial services — are grounded systems. Grounding the system fixes the voltage to ground, gives lightning and surge energy a reference, and makes the fault-clearing path on the 250.4 page possible. Whether a delta system is grounded, and which conductor is the grounded one (250.26), is set by this article — never by field preference.
sections.on_the_job: Identify the system before you bond anything: wye or delta, which conductor (if any) is grounded, and where the single grounding point is. On an unfamiliar commercial service, the transformer configuration answers these questions — get it from the drawings or the utility, not by testing until something looks right.
sections.figure_idea: Three service diagrams — 120/240 single-phase, 208Y/120, 480Y/277 — each with the grounded conductor marked and the single grounding point circled.

sections.title: Grounding at the service — and nowhere downstream
sections.plain_explanation:
At the service, the grounded conductor is connected to the grounding electrode system and to the equipment grounding conductors through the main bonding jumper, in the service equipment. That is the one place in a premises system where neutral and ground meet. Downstream of the service — in subpanels and feeders — the grounded conductor is kept isolated from equipment grounds and enclosures, so normal neutral current never travels on metal parts and fault current has one clear path home.

FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

sections.title: Main and system bonding jumpers
sections.plain_explanation:
The bonding jumper is the conductor or connection that ties the grounded conductor, the equipment grounding system, and the enclosure together at the service, and the system bonding jumper does the same job for a separately derived system. This section covers their material and how they are sized — for the main bonding jumper, by reference to the same sizing table used for the grounding electrode conductor, with the limits the section states. A jumper that is present but undersized or poorly landed does not do the job.

The sizing numbers: a main bonding jumper is sized from Table 250.102(C)(1) by the size of the largest ungrounded service conductor (250.28(D)(1)).. Where the service conductors are larger than 1100 kcmil copper (1750 kcmil aluminum), the table stops and the jumper must be not less than 12-1/2 percent of the cross-sectional area of the largest phase conductor. On ordinary house services the table rows are the whole answer: 8 AWG copper behind a 100A service on 4 AWG copper conductors, 4 AWG copper behind a 200A service on 2/0 copper.
sections.on_the_job: Factory-installed straps and screws count only when they are the listed means for that equipment and actually installed. On a service change, verify the jumper exists before you call for inspection — it is a small part with a whole article riding on it.

sections.title: Separately derived systems — generators and transformers
sections.plain_explanation:
A separately derived system (SDS) is a source — a transformer, or a generator whose neutral is switched — that has no direct electrical connection to the supply system's circuit conductors; the two systems touch only through grounding and bonding. Because it is its own system, it needs its own grounding arrangement: a system bonding jumper connecting the derived neutral to the equipment grounds and enclosure, made at the source or at the first disconnecting means — at one point; both are allowed only where doing so does not create a parallel path for neutral current (250.30(A)(1) Exception No. 2). — and a grounding electrode conductor run to the building or structure grounding electrode system, as near as practicable to the point where the GEC connects to the system (250.30(A)(4)). A new rod is only needed where the building has no electrode system., sized from the derived conductors by the same table used at a service (250.66). A ground rod driven beside a generator, without the bonding jumper and electrode conductor, is decoration, not grounding.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 250.30(C): Removed the word "neutral'' from 250.30(C) to be consistent with other locations within the NEC and with language found at 250.36 and 250.187.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: The transfer switch decides the design. If the switch does not switch the neutral, the generator is usually NOT separately derived, and the neutral stays bonded only at the service. If it does switch the neutral, the generator is an SDS and gets its bonding jumper at the generator end. Confirm which design the job has before anyone bonds a generator neutral — two bonding points put neutral current on the grounding path.

sections.title: A separate building fed by a feeder
sections.plain_explanation: When a feeder supplies a second building or structure, that building needs its own grounding electrode system and a disconnect, and an equipment grounding conductor is run with the feeder in modern work. The grounded conductor at the separate building is not bonded again in the ordinary case — the bond stays at the service — and the narrow exception for existing installations has conditions that must all be met. This is the Article 250 companion to the Article 225 pages earlier in this chapter.
sections.on_the_job: Treat a detached garage panel as a subpanel that also needs electrodes: four-wire feeder, isolated neutral, ground bar bonded, rods driven at the building. Do not re-bond the neutral because the building 'feels like' its own service.

sections.title: Portable generators — frame grounding and the neutral bond
sections.plain_explanation: A portable generator is not automatically a separately derived system. Where the generator supplies only equipment mounted on it and cord-and-plug equipment plugged into its own receptacles, the generator frame itself serves as the grounding reference and the Code does not require a ground rod to be driven for it; the frame is bonded to the equipment grounding terminals of its receptacles. Whether the neutral is bonded to the frame depends on the generator's design — bonded-neutral and floating-neutral portables both exist, and they behave differently with GFCI receptacles and transfer equipment. The picture changes when the generator feeds premises wiring: then the transfer equipment and the rules on the 250.30 page decide whether the neutral is switched, where the single bonding point is, and what electrode connection is required.
sections.on_the_job: Read the generator's label before connecting it to a house: 'neutral bonded to frame' versus a floating neutral changes the transfer-switch design. The field failure is a bonded-neutral portable plugged into a system that also bonds at the service — neutral current on the grounding path and nuisance GFCI trips.
sections.figure_idea: Portable generator with its receptacle panel: frame bond shown, neutral-bond label called out, and a crossed-out back-feed cord beside it.
sections.florida_note: Hurricane season makes portable generators a standing Florida case — and homeowners back-feeding a panel through a dryer receptacle is a lethal, illegal arrangement. Sharma's answer is a listed inlet with an interlock or transfer switch, sized and bonded per the design, every time.

sections.title: The grounding electrode system — all of it, bonded together
sections.plain_explanation:
Every grounding electrode that is present at a building must be bonded together into one grounding electrode system: metal underground water pipe, building steel, a concrete-encased electrode, a ground ring, rods and pipes, plates, and the other electrodes the next section lists. 'Present' is the deciding word — an electrode that exists on the job may not be skipped because another one was easier to connect. The grounding electrode conductor connects that system to the service.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 250.50: The term "reinforcing steel or rods" was replaced with "rebar." This revision was done in all three sections of the Code for consistency.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Inventory the electrodes on the site walk: water service material, foundation steel or rebar, and what will be driven. A concrete-encased electrode has to be caught before the pour — after it, the chance is gone.
sections.figure_idea: A foundation plan with a Ufer connection stubbed up, a water pipe bond, and two ground rods, all tied by one conductor back to the service.

sections.title: Electrodes that are permitted — and the ones that are not
sections.plain_explanation:
This section lists what may serve as a grounding electrode, from underground water pipe with its conditions, through building steel and concrete-encased electrodes — at least 20 ft of the stated rebar or bare copper conductor encased in the foundation — to rods, pipes, and plates. It also lists what may not be used, which includes metal underground gas piping and aluminum electrodes. A water pipe electrode has its own supplementing rule, covered with the installation section.

The electrode specifications in numbers:
• Metal underground water pipe — at least 10 ft of pipe in direct contact with the earth
• Concrete-encased electrode — at least 20 ft of 1/2 in or larger rebar, or at least 20 ft of bare 4 AWG copper conductor, encased in at least 2 in of concrete in the footing or foundation
• Ground ring — at least 20 ft of bare 2 AWG copper, buried at least 30 in below grade
• Rod and pipe electrodes — at least 8 ft long in contact with the soil; pipe not smaller than 3/4 in trade size; rods not smaller than 5/8 in diameter unless listed for the use
• Plate electrodes — at least 2 sq ft of surface exposed to the surrounding soil
sections.on_the_job: The concrete-encased electrode is the one to coordinate with the builder: 20 ft of qualifying rebar or conductor, encased as the section requires, with an accessible connection. Confirm it with the concrete crew before the pour, in writing on the job notes.

sections.title: Installing electrodes — rods, depth, and the second rod
sections.plain_explanation:
Electrodes must be installed as this section requires: driven or buried to the depths it states, kept as close as practicable to each other and to the service, and supplemented where a single rod, pipe, or plate does not meet the stated resistance to earth — 25 ohms or less — or is not tested at all. In practice that means a second rod, spaced at least 6 ft from the first, on almost every job. Rod connections must be accessible or of the irreversible or exothermic type the article allows where they are buried.

The installation numbers:
• Rod, pipe, and plate electrodes — at least 8 ft of the electrode in contact with the soil, with the top end flush with or below grade level unless the connection is protected
• Two rods — spaced at least 6 ft apart; the 6 ft is a floor, and wider spacing makes the pair work better
• A single rod, pipe, or plate may stand alone only with a measured resistance to earth of 25 ohms or less — without that measurement on file, the second electrode is required, not optional
sections.on_the_job: Drive two rods at least 6 ft apart unless you have a tested 25-ohm-or-less result in the job file. Keep the grounding electrode conductor run short, straight, and protected where it is exposed.
sections.figure_idea: Two ground rods driven flush, spaced with a 6 ft tape between them, and the conductor clamped to each in turn on its way to the service.

sections.title: Installing the grounding electrode conductor
sections.plain_explanation:
The grounding electrode conductor is sized on the 250.66 page; this section is how it must be run:
• Continuous, in one unbroken length, without a splice or joint — except splices made with irreversible compression connectors listed as grounding and bonding equipment, or by exothermic welding
• Bare or covered aluminum or copper-clad aluminum GECs without an extruded polymeric covering may not be installed where subject to corrosive conditions or in direct contact with concrete; terminations inside listed enclosures identified for the environment are allowed within 18 in. of the enclosure bottom; outside buildings or enclosures, they may not be terminated within 18 in. of the earth
• Where exposed, a conductor 6 AWG or larger may follow the surface of the building construction without a raceway where it is securely fastened and not subject to physical damage; smaller conductors, and any run exposed to damage, must be protected — in rigid metal conduit, IMC, EMT, schedule 80 PVC, RTRC-XW, or cable armor, or another method this section lists
• A ferrous metal raceway or armor enclosing the conductor must be electrically continuous and bonded to the conductor at both ends — an unbonded steel sleeve chokes the fault path it was meant to protect

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 250.64: New 250.64(G): a grounding electrode conductor (GEC) can't pass through an enclosure's ventilation openings. Bring it in through a knockout, hub or other proper opening. A GEC can't pass through a ventilation opening in an enclosure (250.64(G)). Bring it in through a knockout, hub or other proper opening.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Plan the run as one piece from the service to the electrode before anything is cut. A grounding electrode conductor that comes up short gets replaced or extended by an irreversible splice — never by a split bolt that will end up buried in a wall or a trench.
sections.figure_idea: A grounding electrode conductor run from panel to rod in one unbroken line, with a callout at a steel sleeve showing bonds at both ends.

sections.title: Sizing the grounding electrode conductor
sections.plain_explanation:
The grounding electrode conductor is sized from Table 250.66 by the size of the largest service-entrance conductor, not by the amperage of the service disconnect alone. The section then caps what is actually required for particular electrodes: a run that goes only to rods needs no larger than the stated maximum, and a run to a concrete-encased electrode has its own larger cap — the existing checklist and quiz items carry those numbers. Aluminum and copper-clad conductors used for this purpose have material and installation limits in the surrounding sections. The caps, stated plainly: the portion of the GEC that is the sole connection to a rod, pipe, or plate electrode never has to be larger than 6 AWG copper, and the portion that is the sole connection to a concrete-encased electrode never has to be larger than 4 AWG copper.

Table 250.66 itself — read across: size of the largest service-entrance conductor, then the grounding electrode conductor it requires:
• 2 AWG copper or smaller — or 1/0 AWG aluminum or smaller: 8 AWG copper GEC (6 AWG if the GEC itself is aluminum)
• 1 or 1/0 AWG copper — or 2/0 or 3/0 AWG aluminum: 6 AWG copper (4 AWG aluminum)
• 2/0 or 3/0 AWG copper — or 4/0 AWG or 250 kcmil aluminum: 4 AWG copper (2 AWG aluminum)
• Over 3/0 through 350 kcmil copper — or over 250 through 500 kcmil aluminum: 2 AWG copper (1/0 aluminum)
• Over 350 through 600 kcmil copper — or over 500 through 900 kcmil aluminum: 1/0 copper (3/0 aluminum)
• Over 600 through 1100 kcmil copper — or over 900 through 1750 kcmil aluminum: 2/0 copper (4/0 aluminum)
• Over 1100 kcmil copper — or over 1750 kcmil aluminum: 3/0 copper (250 kcmil aluminum)
The electrode caps stated above then limit what a run to one kind of electrode must actually be — the table size governs a run that serves the whole electrode system.
sections.on_the_job:
Read the service conductor size off the actual conductors, then open the table — a 200A service on compact conductors is not automatically the row you expect. Where one conductor serves several electrodes, size and cap it electrode by electrode as the section directs.

The two house rows, worked: a 100A service on 4 AWG copper or 2 AWG aluminum service conductors reads the first row — 8 AWG copper grounding electrode conductor. A 200A service on 2/0 copper or 4/0 aluminum reads the third row — 4 AWG copper. Those two answers cover most Sharma services before the per-electrode caps are applied.

sections.title: Connections to electrodes — accessibility and continuity
sections.plain_explanation:
Grounding electrode conductor connections must be made so they stay effective: clamps and connectors listed for the electrode and the conductor, connections to a water pipe made at an accessible point within the stated distance of where the pipe enters the building, and the conductor kept continuous or spliced only by the methods this section allows. Interior metal water piping farther into the building is a bonding question, not a substitute electrode connection point.

The stated distance, in numbers: interior metal water piping may be used to interconnect electrodes only within 5 ft of the point where the water pipe enters the building. Beyond that first 5 ft the piping is bonded under 250.104, but it is not part of the electrode path.
sections.on_the_job: Land the water-pipe clamp where it can be inspected, on clean metal, and do not bury a mechanical splice in the grounding electrode conductor run. If a run is cut short on a remodel, replace it or use an allowed irreversible splice — not a split bolt in a wall.

sections.title: The intersystem bonding termination
sections.plain_explanation:
Other systems — telephone, cable, antenna, and similar communications systems — need a place to bond to the electrical grounding system, and this section requires an intersystem bonding termination at the service or metering equipment, accessible for connection, with room for the stated number of terminations. It is the small bar or bridge by the meter that keeps a cable installer from clamping onto a random pipe. It does not replace the bonding those systems' own articles require; it gives them the listed place to land.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 250.94(A): Made minor wording changes in 250.94(A)(4) a and band removed Informational Note 1, which did not have much value within the code and did not comply with the NEC Style Manual.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Install it where the other utilities actually arrive at the house, and leave it accessible after siding and landscaping. Point it out on the final walk — half its failures are being buried behind finishes.
sections.figure_idea: A meter base with a small bonding bridge mounted beside it, with telephone and cable ground wires landed on its terminals.

sections.title: Bonding metal piping systems
sections.plain_explanation:
Metal water piping in a building supplied by a grounded system must be bonded, sized and connected as this section directs, and other metal piping that is likely to become energized — gas piping is the standard example — must be bonded as well. The bonding jumper is sized by the circuit or service that could energize the piping, using the tables this section points to. Bonding a pipe is a different job from using it as an electrode, and a pipe can need both treatments in different places.

Which table sizes which bond:
• Metal water piping at a service — the bonding jumper is sized from Table 250.102(C)(1), by the size of the service-entrance conductors (250.104(A)(1)), the same table that sizes the grounding electrode conductor
• Metal water piping in a building supplied by a feeder — sized per 250.102(D), which uses Table 250.122 based on the rating of the feeder overcurrent device (250.104(A)(3))
• Other metal piping, such as gas — the jumper is sized from Table 250.122, by the rating of the circuit that is likely to energize the piping
sections.on_the_job: Trace the water piping bond from the panel to clean pipe, and check any jumper over a water meter or filter so the path stays continuous when the meter is removed. For gas piping, bond per this section and the appliance and piping instructions — and see the Florida note on CSST.
sections.florida_note: CSST gas piping carries manufacturer bonding instructions and FBC Fuel Gas requirements beyond this section. The v1 item L-059 is simplified to this section's rule; do not treat this page as covering CSST bonding.

sections.title: Equipment grounding conductors — what counts as one
sections.plain_explanation:
The fault path back to the source may be a wire, or it may be one of the wiring methods this section recognizes as an equipment grounding conductor:
• A wire-type conductor — copper, aluminum, or copper-clad aluminum, bare, covered, or insulated, run with the circuit conductors
• Rigid metal conduit, intermediate metal conduit, and electrical metallic tubing — the raceway itself is the ground path, which is why its fittings must be listed and made up tight
• The armor of Type AC cable, with its internal bonding strip; and Type MC cable where the armor, alone or combined with its contained grounding conductor, is listed as the ground path
• Flexible metal conduit and liquidtight flexible metal conduit — only within this section's limits on length (6 ft combined in the ground-return path), fitting listing, and overcurrent rating; outside those limits a wire-type ground must be pulled with the circuit
A method not on this section's list is not a ground path, however solid it looks.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 250.118: Stainless steel flexible metal conduit (FMC), and liquidtight flex (LFMC) with a stainless core, can't serve as the equipment grounding conductor (EGC) anymore. Add a wire-type EGC or a bonding jumper. Stainless steel FMC doesn't count as the EGC. Install a wire-type EGC, or a bonding jumper that meets 250.102(E)(2) (250.118(A)(5)(f)).
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: An EMT run with tight listed fittings is its own ground; a loose set-screw coupling is a break in that ground. On a long flexible whip to a motor or rooftop unit, pull the green wire instead of asking the flex to be the path.
sections.figure_idea: Four ground paths drawn side by side: a green wire in conduit, an EMT run with tight fittings, AC armor with its bonding strip, and a flex whip with a wire-type ground pulled inside.

sections.title: Identifying the equipment grounding conductor
sections.plain_explanation: An equipment grounding conductor is identified by its color: continuous green, green with one or more yellow stripes, or bare. For sizes 6 AWG and smaller — and in multiconductor cable, an insulated conductor may be re-identified as the EGC at each end and every accessible point only where maintenance and supervision ensure that only qualified persons service the installation (250.119(B)).; a green conductor may not be re-marked into something else at the ends. For conductors 4 AWG and larger (250.119(A)), an insulated conductor of another color may be identified as the equipment grounding conductor by green marking at each termination and at every point where the conductor is accessible. The reservation runs in both directions: a white or gray conductor is never an equipment ground, and a green conductor is never used as a current-carrying conductor.
sections.on_the_job: In a pull, if the green is missing, the pull is wrong — stop and fix the wire order rather than planning to tape a black conductor green at both ends of a 12 AWG run. Tape-marking is the large-conductor allowance, not a small-wire shortcut.
sections.figure_idea: Conductor lineup: green, green with yellow stripe, and bare marked as approved EGC identification; a black 12 AWG with green tape crossed out; the same tape marking at 4/0 by the lug marked approved.

sections.title: Sizing the equipment grounding conductor
sections.plain_explanation:
The green or bare conductor that runs with a circuit is sized from Table 250.122 by the rating of the overcurrent device ahead of it — not by the size of the current-carrying conductors, except that when circuit conductors are upsized, the equipment ground must be upsized in proportion. It must be able to carry fault current back to the source for as long as the breaker takes to open, which is why a long, upsized run with a standard ground is a defect even though every receptacle tests 'grounded.' The existing quiz items carry the table's common values.

Table 250.122 itself — rating of the overcurrent device ahead of the circuit, then the equipment grounding conductor it requires:
• 15A — 14 AWG copper / 12 AWG aluminum
• 20A — 12 AWG copper / 10 AWG aluminum
• 30A — 10 AWG copper / 8 AWG aluminum
• 40A — 10 AWG copper / 8 AWG aluminum
• 60A — 10 AWG copper / 8 AWG aluminum
• 100A — 8 AWG copper / 6 AWG aluminum
• 200A — 6 AWG copper / 4 AWG aluminum
• 300A — 4 AWG copper / 2 AWG aluminum
• 400A — 3 AWG copper / 1 AWG aluminum
• 500A — 2 AWG copper / 1/0 aluminum
• 600A — 1 AWG copper / 2/0 aluminum
• 800A — 1/0 copper / 3/0 aluminum
• 1000A — 2/0 copper / 4/0 aluminum
• 1200A — 3/0 copper / 250 kcmil aluminum
The table continues to 6000A for large commercial work. Where one equipment ground serves several circuits in a raceway, it is sized for the largest overcurrent device among them.
sections.on_the_job: When you upsize a run for voltage drop, upsize the ground in the same proportion and write both sizes on the plan. Cable assemblies do this for you; conduit runs do not — check the pull list.
sections.sharma_note: S-10: on a CCA branch run, the equipment grounding conductor and its connectors still have to be suitable for the installation — check AL-CU markings where CCA is involved.
sections.figure_idea: A conduit pull list showing a circuit upsized from 12 to 10 AWG for a long run, with the equipment ground upsized beside it.

sections.title: Frames of ranges and dryers on existing circuits
sections.plain_explanation:
New work is 4-wire: the frames of ranges, wall-mounted ovens, counter-mounted cooking units, clothes dryers, and the outlet or junction boxes on their circuits connect to the equipment grounding conductor. This section keeps the older 3-wire arrangement lawful only for an existing branch circuit where no equipment grounding conductor is present in the outlet or junction box, and only if all four conditions are met: the supply is 120/240-volt, single-phase, 3-wire, or 208Y/120-volt from a 3-phase, 4-wire wye system; the grounded conductor is not smaller than 10 AWG copper or 8 AWG aluminum; that conductor is insulated, or uninsulated only as part of a Type SE cable on a circuit originating at the service equipment; and the grounding contacts of receptacles furnished as part of the equipment are bonded to the equipment.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 250.140: Old 3-wire range and dryer circuits fed with service-entrance (SE) cable from a panel that isn't the service can keep using the neutral for the frame, once the bare neutral is covered. New 250.140(B)(5): existing SE cable from equipment other than the service can bond the frame through its neutral, if that neutral is insulated or covered.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: On a service call, identify what is actually in the wall before quoting a receptacle swap. If the circuit is being replaced or extended as new work, pull 4-wire and set a 4-wire receptacle and cord; never create a new 3-wire installation, and never leave the strap in place on a 4-wire hookup.
sections.figure_idea: A dryer back panel showing the bonding strap removed and a 4-wire cord's green lead landed on the frame screw.
